div.head: MODOIJG-4141'S PARRINT SELF-RISING FLOUR ILEIMIT
div.p: MODOIJG-4141'S PARRINT SELF-RISING FLOUR ILEIMIT
ILLUSTRATED FASHION S.

There is a decided feeling this season for soft materials, and soft harmonies of colour. Indeed, the wise woman in whatever station of life she may be will avoid anything bright, and there- fore remarkable, as regards her dresses. One gets -so soon tired of wearing a very gay dress. which is sure to become well-known to one s Circle of friends and acquaintances a very undesirable state of affairs altogether. A pratty dress of some soft shade only leaves an. impres- sion of pleasantness in the minds of the behold- ers, and does not date itself, so to speak. My advice to all whose dresses have to do service for at least one season, is to sternly resist any inclination towards any marked feature of fashion which may be in vogue at the time of selection while remaining up-to-date as much as possible. Indeed, there is really nothing so useful as a black voile or cashmere dress made over a s.ice lining (silk preferably) for the trimmg, of such a toilette can be varied so readily, and the addition of more or less lace will always have a smart result. The pretty linen d-4 depicted is expressed in the new shade of Slue which is half-way between electric and rrneher's blue, and is one of the most approval colours this summer. It

is trimmed with strappings of its own selvedge in black and white, which is most effective. it is arranged in graduated widths round the foot of the skirt as far as the knees, and again down the front of the bodice which opens over an Irish lace vest. There is no collar-band, the throat being left uncovered except for a narrow band of black velvet ribbon. It is really much more healthful to leave the throat exposed as is now so much done, only a transparent band of lace being occasionally worn. The fashion of a few years ago of enveloping the throat in swathings of lace or ribbon induced many throat ailments and chronic weakness, for, when evening dress was worn, and the throat exposed, one was almost certain to catch cold. A string of pearls is often worn with the collart-ss bodices, for there is nothing so becoming as these gems, whether real or imitation. Silk linen is the material this season, and is usually of the blue tone previously described, or of the numer- ous pretty shades of cerise, rieux rose, or tomato, while green of the tint of the early spring leaves, or in a dull artistic shade, is occasionally to be met with. White and cream are also much in evidence. Deep shades of ivory, champagne. and oatmeal are more fashionable and popular still;
Lace was never so much in demand as at a present time. Everything is more or li- trimmed with lace, especially millinery. Th,

CSHARMING. HAT. old fashion of draping the hat brim with lace •has been revived, and a charming sample is given in the hat illustrated, which is also trimmed with shaded roses and a white ostrich plume curling to the front. There is all the difference in the world, however, between the new lace-draped toques and those which were en evidence in the early sixties. Irish guipure is, perhaps, one of the most fashionable lace-,
this seaso-n; and it appears on hats and toques . _ _

more than any other kind of lace. Never was • there such a fancy for flat headgear as at the present time, and some of those to be seen marked "Parisien " are more outré than pretty. The tricorne hat is another favourite for travel- ling or morning wear. It is very becoming to some faces and is generally very smart wear. A particularly successful. one I saw was of white chip with the edges bound with black velvet, while a swathing of white illusion surrounded the crown and a compact little bunch of little wild Alpine strawberries with a few of their own blossoms and small green leaves was placed at either side. The tricorn° hat to be correctly worn should have the point projecting well over the forehead. This kews the veil out from the face (a great advantage) the fulness being gathered rouni the brim and the lower edge brought closely under the chin. Some people are wearing the veil only to the tip of the nose, but this is not generally fashionable.
The net slip depicted is of a deep cream tone and is covered with tiny spots. It is trimmed
A NET

with a little Valenciennes lace and insertion to match, and is made in an extremely pretty style. The front from the yoke downwards is covered with tiny lace-edged frills, while the sleeves, which terminate at the elbow, finish in a series of tiny frills of the same description. This mode is rather out of the ordinary, while not very elabo- rate. Blouses of lace and lace entirely are still much worn, although it is noticeable that there is a tendency towards having the bodice to match -the skirt. A distinct novelty in blouses this season is the blouse with the coat basque at the back, but, indeed, it is hard to define when the blouse ceases and the bodice takes it place. Thin Chinese silk blouses with transparent lace yokes are _much worn, and are delightfully cool wear, and have the advantage of going with any kind of skirt. Tuck- ings are much used for the ornamentation of blouses, some, indeed, being entirely covered with the tiniest possible tucks. These often cover the sleeve as well with here and there a band of lace insertion to relieve the severity.
COQUETTS.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Kleg's colossal dinner party to half a million of the London poor, was most succssefully carried out. It was obviously no small undertaking, but the arrange- ments were all that could be desired. and the knowledge that the King was on the high road to recovery, added greatly to the festivity of the feast and e ccompanying entertainmecte. There were sr mething like eleven hun- dred different places of entertainment, and as many of these 33 possible were visited during the afternoon by members of the Royal Family. The Prince and Prir cess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Cony aught, the Duee and Duchess of Fife, the Duchess of Argyll, and, in fact, with the exception of the King and Queen. all the mem- bers of the Royal Family were engaged in this way, in affording the utmost gratification to his Majesty's guests. Througheut the long roll of Ergiish history, the Edwards have generally been unlucky. and many people who believe in omens regarded the King's assumption of the title of Edward VII, as certain to bring Mif- fortune upon his Majesty. Of the six past Kings of that name, two were murdered, and two died young, whi st many other instances could be quoted showing that Edward has been an unfortunate name in the Royal line,even down to the Duke of Clarence who was also an Edward. The Ring's illnesietwo days before the appointed time for his Coronation, wi I therefore confirm the presenti- ments of those superstitiously inclined. Many are also disposed to regal d Sunday ass fateful day in the life of , the King—as it was on that day that he car tracted I typhoid fever in 1871—end it was on the first day of the ' week that his Majesty slipped on the staircase at Lord Rothsehild's house, and was laid up for some weeks with an injured knee. Again, it was on a Sunday, that be was shot at by Sipido in Brussels, and a similar ' coincidence marked the commencement of the crisis in his Majesty's present illness. Lady Burdett-Coutts, who is in her eighty-eighth year folly intended to he present at the stately Pageant of the Coronation, and in spite of her years, she retains a large share of her physical and mental activity. Her life history, like that of the ex-Empress Eugenie would fill volumes, and embrace events which scarcely seem in these days to belong to modern times. It is a far cry from the coronation of William IV, to the Coronation of Edward VII, and yet the Baroness has a clear recollec- tion of all the great public events of that long period. In most of these she has hereelf taken part and only the other day she supplied all the ferns, flowers,and decora- tions for the Central Hall at the Courts of Justice on the occaeien of the King's dinner to the poor of the Strand district. Lady Burdett-Coutts' house in Stratton-street was also beautifully illurninated as it was at the time of the Diamond Jubilee when crowds of people flocked to see it. Every year someone comes forward with the advice that we should spend our holidays at home instead of going abroad. The appeal is usually made on patriotic grounds, but it might also be considered on the score of health. Sea-air and holiday repose are the best remedies for nervous distress, and depression, and those who merely want to recuperate need go no further than the coast line, to enjoy these benefits. To ep,nd half the week in travelling and the ether half in violent sightseeing, one needs to be in thoroughly good health before starting on such a fatiguing task. Many people who are a bit run down would therefore do better to spend their holidays at home, instead of still further exhausting their strength by the trials and worries of foreign travelling. The Duke and Duchess of Fife and their children, will spend most of the summer on the East Coast, and have taken Kingsgate BOUM near Ramsgate for the season. Their Royal Highnesses share the very common belief in the recuperative powers of the air of the North Sea, and it is not improbable that his Majesty the King will go to I the neighbourhood of the North Foreland, to obtain the benefit of its health-giving properties. Though net far from the popular eeeside resorts of Margate and Rams- gate, Kingsgate remains unspoilt by the trippers, and the district is not without historical associations. It I was at Pierremont, since turned into a echo. 1, that our late Queen, then Princess Victoria, of Bent. stayed many months with her mother, the Duchess of Kent. There are hundreds and thousands of children attend- ing the schools in London who never see the country from one year's end to another. end it was a happy idea that originated the Children's Flower Fund for encourag- ing and enabling children in the country, to send parcels of flowers from the woods and fields to children in town. Last year the fund, of which Lady Way is president, was the means of forwarding some six or seven hundred boxes of flowers to London schools, thus serving the double purpose of decoration, and an object lesson in the names and beauty of many of our wild flowers. No doubt there are numbers of people who would be willing to aesiq in this work, if they were ac- quainted with the aim and object of the fund, and further particulars will readily be given by Messrs Beard 20, Christchurch-road. Hampstead, London, N.W. The water picnic at Henley usually brings forth some lovely gowns, as, given fine weather the lawns and houseboats afford ample opportunities for the display of the most elaborate muslin and laces. For ordinary boating wear, linens are very popular, tut soft woollen fabrics are preferable, as they do not crush and get out offerder like the Hamm In any cue only the soft, silky linens should be made up, as if not exactly unorusbable, they do not tumble and crease so mach, and one sees , same vrry dainty confections built of the new'art linens. ' In muslin, linen, and indeed all light-weight mstorials the three-decker skirt is in conniderab'e fume. Per- vided a good pattern is forthcoming, this is not so diffi- cult to build as BOMA home workers anpear to think, and provided the wearer is a little above the averaee height, It proves almost invariably tecoming. The three ffonneea—sho wing scarcely any fulnes‹—must, to be correct—be edged with curved stranpings of silk, either matching' rr in contrast, to the material. On the little bolero, which usually accompanies such a skirt, and on the sleeves, the stres,pings should again appear. I All sorts and conditions of both sexes have this year taken to wearing the Panama hat, but, with very few exceptions, it is no more becoming to women than to men. It is only the swarthy ginsy countenance that appears to advantage under the Panama hat, Fortun- ately though a good Panama is expensive, its counterfeit can be bought for a few shillings!, and already it has become mere übiquitous than fashionable. No doubt it will also be discarded by the opposite sex, as the moat casual observer can hardly have failed to notice how much less:beeoming it is to men than the old fashioned straw tat.
MADGE.

The r ming Austrian noble, Prince Francis Joseph of Bracer n, a lieutenant in the Austrian army, appeared again at Southwark Police Court on Wednesday in con- nection with a Perim:is charge of discreditable conduct. Three youths were associated in the same charge. For the defence of the Prince, Sir Edward Clarke said he proposed to bring • charge of conspiracy against the other prisoners. div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY JULY 11 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JULY 11 1902
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
WILM_A.Y,
BY BARRY PAIN.
PART IL-CHAPTER IV.

I started for Ayshurst, of course, as soon as 1 received the telegram. Had Philip been an ordinary man, the telegram would have worried me a good deal. As it was, I was by no means sure that he intended me to take it seriously, and that he would not laugh at me on my arrival. gven if he meant me to come, it was quite possible that it was for some perfectly trivial object. In short, I knew that it might mean anything or nothing. I had telegraphed back to say by what train I was coming. The dog-cart was waiting for me at Ayshurst, and one glance at-the face of the man who drove it was enough to make me ask him what was wrong at Sinden. He told me that there had been a bad accident, that Philip had been terribly hurt, and that it was very doubtful whether he would still be alive on my arrival. The man drove hard, and there was no time to tell me the details before we were at the door of the house. _ _ _ _ _

The door was opened at once, before I could knock or ring, not by Carter, but by an old gentle- man with his cuffs turned back. He was self. possessed, but he spoke quickly. "Mr. Derrimer ?" "Yes. You are the doctor!" "I am Dr. Ingwold. Yoli are just in time. He says that he cannot die until he has seen you." • There is no hope!" "None. There never has been. I have been here since the early morning, when it happened, but I can only make the pain rather less for him. You had better go into him at once." "Yes." I went towards the staircase. The doctor touched me on the shoulder.
"Not upstairs," he said. "He is in the itudy. It would have been cruelty to carry him any further than was necessary." • We went down a passage ;to the study. At the door the doctor said:
.... . "There is a nurse there, but she will come and wait outside with me. He was conscious when I left him."

Within I heard a faint repeated groan. I entered the room. A bed had been put there, and the nurse was just turning away from it with a glass in her hand. Little details in the room seemed as if they would be noticed by me even against my will. There was a black morocco hand. bag on the table, bearing the initials R.H.I. in gilt. I found myself puzzled, and then decided that it must belong to the doctor. There was a faint smell of some antesthetic—l wondered what it was. I noticed a grotesque design in vermilion on an old brown leather screen—was surprised that everything was in order, and that the room was so little changed. All this passed through my mind in a second, as I stepped from the door to the bed- side. The nurse came up to me and asked me to go quite close to the bed so that he need only speak in a whisper. Then she slipped out of the MOM. _ .

Philip lay on the bed. There was only a sheet over him. His torn and broken body could not bear the weight of heavy bed-clothes. A bandage over his forehead had a fantastic effect like a turban. There was death in his face and death in his changed voice. He did not move, but his eyes turned to me. "Thank you for having come, Edward. Every- thing else is settled. I waited only to see you. I wanted a ask you if you would be Wilmay'r guardian?" "Yes. You ihould have been sure of that." _
"I was, but I wanted to ask it. And you'll do the best you can for her." "All that I can."

" il;ai'Tgo-od-01 you. She was here a little while ago, but wouldn't let her stay—scenes like this aren't—we just said good-bye. You take charge of everything. All paperh are in the safe in the library, and Mrs. Blayd will give you the keys." There was a long pause, and then he said: "I'm so sorry that I cannot give you my hand:" I could not answer. I put one hand lightly on his shoulder, watching his face to be sure that it did not hurt him. He seemed to ,become drowsy, his eyes closed, and I do not think he knew any longer that I was in the room. His voice was much weaker; le spoke at intervals, but I did not always hear what he said. Once I caught the words "a long day," and afterwards "and then it becomes much more quiet." Sometimes I heard Wilmay's name. He may have thought that he was speaking to her. Then his lips moved no more, and in the stillness I only heard a watch ticking as if it had gone mad, seeming now to grow louder and now fainter, sometimes to stop for a second and then to hurry on again.

"Philip," I said. - He made no sign that ho had heard me. I stepped softly to the door and opened it. The doctor, the nurse, and Mrs. Zlayd were waiting outside. The doctor and nurse went into the room now, and I waited with Mrs. Blayd. She was a hard-featured woman, a woman with an immobile face that gave no token of her feelings. I asked her how Wilmay was. "She is lying down now, sir. She does not speak, and she seems worn out. The rest will do her good, I hope." "I hope so.' The door opened and the doctor came out, closing the door behind him. "It is all over," he said. His look of relief was undisguised. "Can you see me in the library in a few minutes, Mr. Derrimer!" he asked.

"Certainly," I said. "I will wait for you there." The doctor went back into the room, and I turned to Mrs. Blayd. "Shall I—" I began. "I think," she said, "that it would be better if I told Wilmay. And—there are other little things to be done—some orders—l could see after all that for you." I thanked her. "And would you tell Wilmay that I will come up and see her, if she would like it?" . "Yes, sir, I will tell her. But Ido not think she would wish to see anybody at all just now. Shalt I press her to—" "No, no. It must be just as she likes. 13ut you Will let her know that I am here."

I Went into the library, thought for a moment, and then wrote a note to my married sister, telling her what had happened, and asking her to come on the morrow. I rang, and had the letter sent off to the post. It was a warm summer day, but I had turned strangely cold. I sat and shivered, waiting for the doctor. It was an hour before he came—it seemed to me to be much longer. He apologised for having kept me waiting. He had been detained.

"A fool of a housemaid had violent hysterics, and another of the maids followed the lead. How- ever, they're all right now, and professionally there is nothing more for me to do. But I should like to stop here to-night, because I think I can be of assistance to you. I knew Amory well—very well, considering that I knew him only during the last three years. If I can do anything to carry out his wishes now, I am glad to have the opportunity. He asked me to stop with you, and he gave me some directions.. Will you have me

"It is very -kind of ion," I said. "Frankly, l do not even know what has to be done on such occasions. I shall be glad both of your advice and companionship. But will it not be taking up toc much of your time ? " "Not at all. My assistant can very well look after my regular practice; this is quite a small village, and there is not very much to do. I leave most of it to my assistant generally. Then that h settled."

He rang the bell. "Carter, I shall be dining and sleeping here to-night. Could you send b message across to my house to tell my man to pack my things and bring them here?" Then he turned to me. "And what have you done so far?"

"Hardly anything. I have written to my married sister, Mrs. Enterland." "Yes. Amory spoke of her to me sometimes." "I think she will come here to-morrow. She b very fond of Wilmay, and I fancy that Wilmay would be quite willing to go away with her." "That, I think, is quite right. Indeed, I dial' think it quite right if you take her away altogether She is an impressionable child, and should be away from the scene—from anything that reminds her. But we shall all miss her here.'

"Do you know how she is?" "I have just asked Mrs. Blayd. She says that she is not ill, but keeps to her room—will not see anyone." He mentioned to me some papers in the library safe, of which Mrs. Blayd has the keys. I should, perhaps, look over them to see if there is anything which needs immediate attention." "Yes, that should be done to-niiht. Amory often told me that he wished to be cremated, and with as little fuss as possible, but there may be further directions." - - _ -
A servant brought in a message that Mrs. Blayd
woum he much obugen It 1 coma speak to her thr a minute. "Very well," I said; "I will see Mrs. Blayd in the dining-room." • She handed me the keys, hesitated, and then said:
"It was about Wilmay, sir, that I winted to speak." " Well ?" "She is not in the house, and I do not know where she has gone."

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.

"I don't understand," I said. "DO you know why she has gone ? " "The same thing happened once before, sir, about two years ago. She was very angry with herself for something, and she went away like this. She was away then for eight hours." "Eight hours ? Was she not found and brought back before that ? " _ _

"Mr. Amory would not permit anyone to go and look for her. He told me She was free to go in and out as she liked, and that she was able to take care of herself. He said, tpo, that if enquiries were made about her, she would become the subject of a good deal of silly talk in the villa,ge, and neither he nor Wilmay would like that. She went in the morning, and it was ' after dinner when she returned. No one but Mr. Amory and myself knew of it, and neither of us said anything to her about it."

"Yes, yes, Mrs. Blayd," I said. "But the case is different now. The poor child is half mad with grief. What you have told me makes me very anxious. And it is already getting late. I think a search should be made for her—with all possible discretion, of course, and without creating talk, but still it seems to me that something must be done." "Very well, sir," said Mrs. Blayd, but she said it doubtfully. • "Well," I said, "you have known Wilmay from her birth. What do you think yourself—what do you really think?" "I think that if we found her now it would be of no good. She is not herself. If we let her have her way, she will stop out to-night, but she will coine . back to-morrow morning. She does not forget those who are fond of her. She would come back if it were only for your sake, sir, or my own. I feel sure of it." . .

It seemed to me to be rather a difficult position. If I did not go to find Wilmay and bring her back, I was not taking proper care of her; and if I did, I was acting contrary to the wishes of her dead father.

"Wait," I said to Mrs. Blvd.- -" I shall ask Dr. Ingwold what he think i would be best.'' The doctor was of the same opinion as Mrs. Blayd. "It may do her some slight temporary harm to stop out all night—but, well, I know her, and I think it more likely to do her good." So we settled that, at any rate, until to-morrow morning, nothing sin:mid be done. From Dr. Ingwolol, later in the same evening, I heard so, :le' ails of the accident.

"It is the old story," said the doctor. "Your nervous, timid whip, who does 'not really under- stand horses, never comes to any harm. He takes no risks. It is the men 'ho really can drive, who really can do a good deal with a horse, that always try to do just a little more, and have the accidents. In the early morning Philip had driven out with a horse that had already been a good deal of trouble to him. But it was a valuable animal, and he was anxious to finish its education. He took no one with him, and he said to the 'groom who brought tbe horse round that he should drive to the station, as he had some enquiries to make there. The groom noticed that, because he knew the horse would not stand sight or sound of .a railway train, and knew that Philip was well aware of it, too. It was three miles away from the railway station that Philip was afterwards found • there was a steep embankment there at one side of the road, with a white painted wood fence by way of protection. Cart, horse and man were found at the bottom of this embankment, and the fence, which seems to have been rotten, was all broken down. Philip did not explain exactly how it happened; he said only that he thought it had been mostly his own fault."

Dr. Ingwold was of great assistance to me, and took on himself the trouble of all the horrible business connected with death. As it grew later, and Wilmav did not return, I again became very anxious about her. I was afraid that she might come back ana tmci the house- shut up ana every- body asleep. I arranged, in consequence, that I would Bit up that night in the library. The library windows opened on to The upper terrace of the garden. I drew the shutters back from these win- dows, and had the lamp placed near them, so that at whatever hour Wilmay returned she might be able to see that I was still up. The doctor went to bed, but said that he would be down very early in the morning to take my place, and give me a chance of an hour or two's sleep. I had found in the safe several papers addressed to me. I put them on the table by the lamp, drew up my chair, lit my pipe, and began to open and read them. There was a terrible quiet in the house, almost as if the inanimate house knew that a dead man was lying there. So much did this idea impress me that the rustling of the papers, or the noise made by the shifting of my chair, seemed to be like a profanity. One gets into a nervous, izagaitinc thenaltiastsaittes up lheanteoanteniigsh. emotionally worn At the tuna that I was reading I vatalso listen- ing intently. If the branches of the trees outside moved in the light wind, the sound seemed changed to Wilmay's voice, and I looked up from the papers. At any moment I was ready to hear her step on the gravel outside, to open the window, and call to her. But she never came. The long hours wore on, tediously long, until the dawn came, and outside in the garden the whispered ,Aiirpings of the birds broke into full song in the sunlight. Amongst the papers there was a copy hl his will, the will itself being in the charge ot is solicitors. .: I knew that he had arranged tor h !tor to act as his executers, because he had oi ten referred to this. "I may," he used to say, "have bored people during my lifetime. I will go further, and say that when I have got on to any of my hobbies, such as precious stones, or emendations in the Agamemnon, or horse-breaking "—and thii by no means exhausted the list of his special subjects— "l must have boil"ed people. In fact, I've seen them get restlers, and smile, and try to look intelli- gent, and have known that I was boring them, and yet been unable to stop it. But I don't mean to go on boring posthumously. I don't mean to ask a man of leisure to do badly for nothing what a man of business can be paid to do well." I did not even glance over the will that night. lam not precisely a sentimentalist, but I was in no hurry to find out what.money the dead Irian had, or what he had done with it.

There was a long letter, addressed to me, and dated only a couple of months before. It began by referring to the uncertainty of life, "oven for a man living as quietly, carefully, and unexcitingly as myself." It went on with his request that I would be Wilmay's guardian, and here, where I would have welcomed the most minute and elaborate directions, he gave none, or next to none. There were only a few suggestions. One, which had already occurred to me, was that Wilmay should go to live with my sister, Mrs. Enterland. He also suggested that, though it might become necessary now to put restrictions on her in some ways, she should still be allowed to work out .her own education just as she liked. In. concluding, he gave me a little—a very little—information. His wife's maiden name had been Wilmay Forland ; she had died very soon after her daughter's birth. "She was the best woman in the world," he wrote, simply, "and, I think, one of the most beautiful. I had no opportunity to get her portratt painted, and we both disliked photographs. That has not mattered, for I have always remembered her, and, as the younger Wilmay grows up, I think you will be able to see what her mother was like." He went on to say that after his death he believed that Wilmay would have no other relation living, though there might possibly be one—her mother's brother. This man's name was Charles Forland. "Before I arrived on the scene I am afraid he was in far from comfortable circumstances. He had already spent his own small capital and the greater part of his sister's. He was still getting money from her, from time to time, in order that he might in future, as he phrased it, adopt a quite different course.' But these sums were of neces• city small, and apparently, after paying for his bare livelihood and the few little luxuries that he felt he could fancy, they left no margin for the adoption of the quite different course. In•addi- lion to this, his sister had entirely ceased to believe in him or respect him.- His conduct was not, it is true, of a kind to make one think that he respected himself, but it was always quite obvious that he liked others to respect him, and would do anything to secure that respect except deserve it. When I appeared on the scene, I was fortunately able to change his circumstances. I wrote him cheques, As I became richer, I wrote him larger cheqaes. I cannot claim that I have ever been able to wsite

mm cneques so large as to make mm feel justinea in the adoption of the quite different course. But I have enabled him to live in comparative affluence without working for it. The only thing that he was required to do for it was to abstain from seeing my wife or daughter, and to see me only on pay- day, when he called for his cheque. Ido not say that I (respected him or believed in him, am he would have liked. But I paid him to keep away, which he seemed to like still better. The last time I saw him was at Sinden, rather more than three years ago. He had called to suggest that he had been put to great personal inconvenience and expense by my move to England, and that the price of his passage both ways should be added to the customary amount of his cheque. It struck me at the time that he gave every promise that he would die of drink in the course of the year. But I. did not like to be too sanguine about it; Charles For- land rarely stuck to any one thing for long. Since then I have not seen him, and I am quite sure he is dead. If he had been alive, he would have been to me for money, and the absence of any demands from him is equivalent to his certificate of death. It was I confess, always amazing to me that he and Wilmay were brother and sister, children of the same parents. But such things happen. He has never seen my daughter Wilmay since she was a baby, by the way, and Wilmay neither recollects him nor knows of his existence. She had better not be told about him. Should he turn up again— but he will not. As I say, I have the equivalent of his death certificate. But do not let me imply that Charles Furland had no good points. He blackmailed me for having married his sister, and he would do no kind of work, and later in life he seems to have become excessiyely intemperate. But he was a handsome man, a good talker, and occasionally a wit—a man by no means without charm." I read the whole of that letter with great interest twice over. I glanced through some of the other papers. At five o'clock I heard footsteps overhead, and then Dr. Ingwold Caine down and entered the library to taketmy place, sending me up to bed at once.

div.head: CIIAPTER VI.
div.p: CIIAPTER VI.

I had not expected to sleep, but I fell asleep at once. I suppose I was about tired out. For rather over two hours I slept soundly, and then woke suddenly, with a start, with the idea that I had just heard Wilmay Call me loudly by my name. It was, of course, a delusion—l had been dreaming. But though I recognised that, I was unable to go to sleep again, and rose. I joined the doctor at breakfast. Wilmay had not returned. For the first time the doctor looked a little hesitating, a little less as if he knew exactly the right thing to do, and was perfectly able to do it. We sent for Mrs. Blayd, and had a long talk with her. She told us of two or three places near, where Wilmay had always been fond of going, and ,where she might possibly be found now. I decided that we would try those places first, and that then if we did not find her, there was no help for it, and a regular search would have to be instituted with all the assistance that we could get. To this Mrs. Blayd quite agreed ; like the doctor, she was beginning to get nervous. The poor woman had, it appeared, herself been up most of the night, awl herself looked worn and ill.

The morning was glorious—a cool wind, a bril- liant sun, and the country as beautiful as if no one had ever died or been unhappy. The doctor and I decided to go first to a plantation standing on the ridge of a low hill about a mile away from Sinden. He went up to the plantation on one side of this ridge, and I on the other.. We were out of sight of each other, but within call. One's footsteps were absolutely noiseless on the soft white sand of the narrow winding path. At the first turn in this path my search was over. Wilmay was coming down the path towards me. She carried a great bunch of wild roses tied together with the riband that she had taken from her hair. The dust had Powdered thick on her little tan shoes ; her pretty hands had been slightly torn and scratched by the brambles. Her face was white, and her lips almost colourless. She smiled when she saw me, and belled me by my name. " Wilmay," I said, "poor little Wilmay ! lam glad I have found you." • "I was coming back," she said. "You very nearly frightened us." "Yes, I have been thinking about that. I would not have been away so long only I wanted to get quite quiet again. That is why I came here, where there isn't anybody. I will be good now." "It's all right, dear ; I didn't mean to find fault with you. It's all right now that we have got you back again. Aren't you very tired?" "Not very. I slept for a little time, until the sun on my eyes woke me. Then I got these." She held out the roses. r'" They are lovely," I said. . . . _ . .

She put them in my hand. " I want you to give them to my father with my dearest love. I shall not see him any more, not any more now." Her voice was wistful and sad, but quite steady. I think she had made up her mind not to cry any more—that she thought it might distress us to see her crying. We walked a few steps further, and I was just going to tell her that I had the doctor with me, when she said : _

"I've suddenly got tired, Edward. Will you— help me a little ? ' I caught her in my arms as she fainted, and put her down on the grass by the path. In a minute I hacrthe doctor by her side. He had come prepared for this emergency, and he soon revived her. When her eyes opened again, she seemed surprised to see him.
"I thought it was Edward," she said. "It was—l am here too." "I'm so sorry—but I can walk again." We would not let her walk, and I carried her the rest of the way.

Before mid-day Bertha arrived, and I was never more glad to see her. She'had given up a host of social engagements, and was prepared to give up any number more for Wilmay's sake. It was the greatest sacrifice that could have been demanded of her, and she made it most willingly. She heard from me, and heard with composure, of Philip's death, hut she could not bear to hear how Wilmay had gone away to the plantation "where there isn't anybody," and how I had found her. She stopped me, and said that a crying woman would be of no good in the house, and she would hear the rest some other time. She spent mist of her time that day with Wilmay, and two days afterwards gave up the rc.-it of the London season and took Wilmay away to the sea. Wilmay was quite willing to go; she had grown very fond of Bertha. They spent the whole of that winter abroad together, and I was with them some part of the time. Youth is recuperative; one blow might take its strength and spirit and gladness for a time, but youth will.have them all back. Wilmay became the old Wilmay again, saw life with her blue eyes as bright as before, rodeher pony, learned to swim and to fence, and chattered the prettiest French without ever learning it at all. "She is at the awkward age," said Bertha some time afterwards to me, "but with the awkward- ness left out. In a few years' time I shall have to begin to think---" Bertha paused. "A beauty, four thousand-a year, and the sweetest nature in the world. She ought to do very well." "There's a splendid auctioneer lost in yen," I said.
Bertha said that was merely rude. "Well," I said, "at any rate wait until the time comes."

"Of course I never breathe a word to her about it—my lord the guardian." "I should think not. And when the time comes, remember that Wilmay has not an atom of worldli- ness in her nature." " Sior have I," retorted Bertha, "only a little common sense."

"You can call it what you like, but I won't have her—when the time does come—forced into any- thing, however brilliant." "You don't understand these things," said my sister, with a sigh of resignation, "but as the child's not yet sixteen, you needn't begin to trouble your guardianish mind just yet." On Wilmay'e sixteenth birthday, she, Bertha, awl myself dined toghther at Bertha's house. There was no one else there. We had dined together in that way many a time before, bttt this evening—this evening for the first time—it was different. (To be continued. )
Grocers are just as good bankers for us as anybody. They give you back your money if you don't like Fels-Naptha soap. 2 12, d a bar. It's our money.
FELS-NAPTHA 39 Wilson Street London EC

div.head: GREAT SAN KEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: GREAT SAN KEY PARISH COUNCIL.
The Chairman Leaves the Meeting.

A meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council was summoned for Tuesday evening. At the appointed time, the only member of the Parish Council present was Mr Thompson, the Chairman. He in company with the Clerk and three representative of the press sat round the table in the Board Room at the Great Sankey Board Schools until ten minutes past eight. No other member put in an appearance and akthere seemed little likelihood of a quotutn being formed, the Chairman postponed the meeting and left the room. Immediately afterwards, fourVpmbers of the Council came down to the school togtner and they were informed that the Chairman had adjcurned the meeting. The four mem- bers consulted tnescher and decided to go on with the meting. Mr J Fulton Smith, the vice-chairman, was appointed to take the chair and there were also present: Mr T Halton, Mr J Kilshaw arid Mr H Singleton, with Mr J Smith (clerk).

div.head: BURGLARY AT THE SCIOOLS.
div.p: THE BURGLARY AT THE SCIOOLS.

The Clerk read the following letterilT-ZOunty Police Office, Leigh. 9th May. Dear sir, I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 7,h mat, and thank you and the members of your Council for the resclution palmed at therr meeting on the 6th, thanking P.S. Harris and P.C. Houghton for the recent capture of two men for breaking ioto the schools at Sark y, and am glad to know that tie services of the two officers are so highly appreciated by your Council, and shall be glad to make this known to the officers cimmerrif cl.—Yours faithfully, M COCKER, superintendent."

div.head: POLICE_ STATION.
div.p: THE POLICE_ STATION.

A second letter ;;vas-r-e;:e1--fi;;;17h.e. Superintendent, stating that after careful inquiry ALI d consideration it was considered very desirable that the constable should be posted at Sankey Bridges. The population, perman- ent and floating within easy distu ce of Constable Dug- dale's station was very Much in excess of that near Great Sankey Station. Mr Halton announced that the Police Sergeant was about to retire.
Regret was expressed at this iniimatiqn and it was decided to write to the Ccunty authorities on the matter. THE LIGHTING OF "ANICEY BRIDGES STATION.

The Clerk read the following let er on this subject . " London and Nora. -Western Railway. General Man- ager's Office, Euston Stati‘m, Le.didon, N.W. Dear sir, —Your letter of she 22nd March htst ealling attention to the lighting of tho company's premises at Sankey Bridges, addressed to Mr Andrews was forwarded to me. I beg to inform you that the matter has been con- sidered,and that ths company is not at present prepared to light the Sankey Bridges station with gas, but in- structions have been siven for a lamp to be fixed on a column to improve the lighting of the approach road. Yours faithfully, F HARRISON." The Clerk reported that the lamp had been erected.

div.head: CORONATION:-THE POSTPONED CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: THE CORONATION:-THE POSTPONED CELEBRATIONS.

The Chairman remarked that the arrangement; Which had been in progress for cel, bating, on the Ist July, the Coronation of the King, wee postponed on account of the untoward illness of his Majesty. That hluess certainly caused a groat deal of regret to his faithful subjects. He thought it would have been better if the festivities at Sankey had been gone on with, esprcially as his Majesty had expressly stated that it was his wish that the festivities in the country should go on. What prompted that message was bis consideration far the poor and the children. (Bear, hear.) The local Corona- tion Committee were fortunate enough, however, not to compromise themselves in their arrangements with the various tradesmen, an that the parish had not been in any wan involved in unnecessary expenditure. No doubt an opportunity would he afforded the parish later on of celebrating the Coronation, and then he hoped the arrangements would he carried out with the utmost good faith, unanimity of purprse,and with the intention of conferring the greatest happiness on the greatest number. (Hear, hear.) Mr Halton severely criticised the action of Mr Thompson with reference to the appointment of a ladies committee for making arrangements for the Coronation celebrations in Great Sankey. Considerable friction had trim and be moved a resolution that another ratepayers' meeting be called for dissolving the Coronation Festivi- ties Committee and appointing a fresh committee. Mr Kilshaw seconded the resolution. _
The Chairman said the ratepayers' meting could be called when there was more definite news about the Coronation. VIN WICK ASYLUM AND THE SEWAGE QUESTION. SANKEY BROOK TO ISE PURIFIED.

Mr Halton reported that the Winwick Asylums Board had been prevented by the Local Government Board from turning their crude sewage into Sankey Brook. The other day he (the speaker) visited Winwick Asylum and learnt that the sum of £4,000 was to be spent in laying down septic tanks. The Local Government Board were compelling other authorities—the Warring- ton Rural District Council, the Corporation of Warring- ton and the St Helens people—who vere polluting Sankey Brook, to stop doirg so, so that it was hoped in a short time Sankey Brook would be quite pure and clean ! He thought the Warrington Corporation and the Rural District Council would be willing to treat their own Effluent befcre long. He thought the Great Sankey Parish Council had reason to be satisfied with the action it had taken in drawing the attention of the Local Government Board to the matter. (Hear, hear). The Chairman : In view of the great improvement which will be made, I believe I may get my fishing tackle in order. (Laughter.).

Mr Halton said no one outside the Rural District Council would have known of the intended action of the :Asylums Board if he had nothnaee it public.He was glad to think that uction had been taken to prevent such a nuisance.

div.head: LIFE IN A FACTORY. ---- Touching Story of a Lancashire Lass.
div.p: LIFE IN A FACTORY. ---- Touching Story of a Lancashire Lass.

The toiler, whose lot it is to have to rise with the lark,summer and winter alike, and then plod hard until night-fall amid the hot,enervating odours of the factory knows only too well how liable he or she is to diseases of the lungs. div.head: BOATING FATALITY ON THE DEE.
div.p: BOATING FATALITY ON THE DEE.
A Picnic Party Run Down. ---- Rev. A. A. Markham in Charge.

A shocking accident occurred on the Dee, on Monday night, by which two lade lost their lives. The choir of St. Jecie's Church, Liverpool, on Monday had a trip le the Dee, and part of the programme was to row up ti river to Eceleston, a few miles tram Chester, and have tea. The Rev Algernon A Markham, (Vicar of St Jude's and formerly curate-in-charge of Sr. Clereent't Mission, Warriegton), and the curate, the Rev. Walter Douglas Auden, were in charge of the party, and hired a large rowing-beat from Messrs Cook and Arthur at The Groves. The party rowed up as far as Eaton, and the return journey to Eccleston was commenced sherfly before five o'clock. The river 'below the Iron Bridge has a very sharp turn, and for entre die. distasee the curves are of a very pronounced nature, and the spot has been the scene of many an upset before. i As much care as possible s yxerci•ed by the captains of steamers and towers at this point, and it is usual for the former to signal the approach of eteamers by sound- ing the whistle. The party had just reached a portion known as the Crooked Dee when the sad accident happened. The steamer Orrnende (Captain Gerrard) eudgenly rounded the ccrner on her lent teen to the Iron Bridge kr the day, and collided with the rowing boat. The latter was capsized and the occupants thrown into the water. The scene naturally was one of the greatest excitement, as the river at this point is very deep. The crew of the steamer rendered all the assistance possible, and one of the clergymen pluckily managed to selze the upturned boat and as,ist fiveilade to board the steamer. The rn.joriZy 'of the otter lads and olergTman reached the shore, and it was only when the muster of the party Was taken that it was dieeovered that two of the lade were missing. The police were informed, and after two hours' grappling both bodies were recovered. The names of the lads drowned are Adolf Ilepnhun, 41, Phythian-street, Liverpool, trod Lancelot Alvey, of North-view, Liverpool. Titarly all the party couA swim, with the exception of the two laes, and it is cssumed that directly the boat capsized they sank.

div.p: WHAT YOU MAY NOT DO IN A
POST OFFICE.

PLacenns in every post office warn the public not to spit, lest they spread Consumption. The infectiousness of Consumption is not full recognised, and the educe-- tion of the public on the danger of spitting only pro gresses slowly. Until this is known, all the King's efforts and all the King's doctors cannot stamp out the scourge. Consumptives must learn not to expectorate on the floor or pavement, for infection is dried up and becomes dust ; as dust it is breathed, and enters a weak chest or a lung deficient iti blood ; a cough is caused, blood-spitting begins, and one more consumptive is started on the road whose end is Death. The one effec- tual way to protect weak chests is by improving the blood supply of the lungs. Consumption is practically draining of blood ; it is a natural follower of anaemia. MR. DAVID ROBERTSON, 99, Springburn-road, Glasgow, a most !respectable, religious man, a member of the Salvation Army, says (and his statement was thoroughly verified) that his life he been on many occasions threat- ened, though not from violence. His doctor said, " Your lungs are done for," He was, in fact, a member of the Consumptive army ! Be thus described his symptoms and his cure by Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people :
Two winters ago I caught a chili, and shortness of breath, a cough, and growing weakness showed

Poultices di not stop the pain nor alleviate the cough, now con- stant, Worse still, there were streaks of blood in the phlegm, which increased PO that I was constantly spit- ting blood. This rapidly reduced my weight and strength, and so weak did I become that I could scarcely stand. I thought myself doomed to the grave. The doctor said I was in a galloping consumption. However, I did not perish, for I had my attention drawn to wonderful cures which bad been effected in consumptives by Dr Williams' pink pills, and I procured some. I was astonished at the change for the better which had Came over me before I bad go" through the second box. First, the pain in my chest left me, then the cough, and I car, hardly describe how thankful I was when I found after two years' suffering and wasting away that I was fast gaining strength and putting on flesh. I continued taking the pills. My appetite returned; I could sleep well at night and awaken refreshed for work. I now mount the - highest stairs, and never feel any ill-effects. There is no spitting of blood. I have gained a stone in weight." Such enthusiasm is not difficult to understand when we remember that Mr Robertson was !Penny snatched from death. A serious railway accident involving severe injuries to a large number of passengers, the wrecking ot two coaches,and considerable damage to the permanent way occurred on the London, Brighton, and South-Coast Railway just outside West Croydon Station, on Wednes- day morning. One youth bad an arm torn right off. The gaol at St Joseph, Missburi, has been partially wrecked by dynamite, three prisoners being responsible. No one was injured. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.
An explosion of gas occurred on Wednesday at Wrex- ham and Acton Colliery, near Wrexham. Seven men were injured, several of tbem severely.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
Cricket

It is but three weeks since Warrington sustained their first reverse of the season at the hands of St Helens. On Saturday the tables were completely turned, the St Helens eleven being thoroughly beaten at Arpley Batting first, the visitors were dismissed for the poor total of 63, and when stumps were drawn at seven o'clock the Warringtonians had compiled 249 for the loss of 8 wickets. Bravo, Warrington!
I

So effective was the Warrington bowling and field- ing, that none of the visiting batsmen attained high figures. Woodley and Ward each knocked up 16, whilst Foreman was responsible for 15. All the other players were dismissed for very small totals. Lynes, the home professional, was in very good form with the ball, capturing 5 wickets at a cost of 37 runs. Connor was responsible for 3 wickets at a cost of 29 runs, and Gibbon for 1 wicket for 2 runs •

P.B. Flawtin was the hero of the afternoon. For a little over two hours and a half he occupied the wicket, and in the end carried out his bat after compiling 84 in excellent style. Changes in the bowling were tried without avail and at times the batsman was loudly cheered. His chief hits included nine fours and three threes.
A meed of praise must also be accorded to J Gibbon who gave a vigorous display for his 50. E A Connor (27), W H Podmore (26), and G Hampson (22), also made useful contributions.
The home professional had prepared an excellent wicket, and the appearance of the pitch was the sub- ject of general comment.

Sankey Wire Mills visited Weaverham and gained a victory by 30 runs. Gough was the top scorer, his innings realizing 25. Good work with the bat was also done by Clarke, J Evans, and Cook for the Wire Mills, and by Moreton and Woodward for Weaverham. Christ Church. Latchford eleven defeated St. Paul's 2nd by the small majority of 7. S Griffiths (12) and W Tomkins (11 not out were the only batsmen to reach double figures. Southern bowled in capital style for Latchford, and accomplished the hat trick.

The match between Latchford Baptists and Grappen- ball 2nd, proved very exciting, Grappenhall running out winners by 5 runs. Mason (21) batted well for the Victors, Callon (201 and Albinson (19) being the top scorers for the Baptists.
Cycling. At the Goodison Park police sports on Saturday, J Mounfield, of Warrington, won the third prize in the , mile bicysle handicap.
Rugby Football

The close season gives very little rest to the managers Of the Northern Union, who have been busy legislat- ing ever since April. On Tuesday the annual meeting oi the Union was held at Huddersfield and after the adoption of a very satisfactory financial report,several alterations of rules were made. Most important of the lot was the abolition of the punt-out from touch, and the substitution of a scrimmage ten yards from touch. There is no doubt that in most .respects the punt-out Was a failure. It ruined centre three-quarter play and tended to increase the quantity of" marks" and kick- ing exchanges which are so irritating and useless. The substituted scrimmage may or may not tend to more open play, but at any rate it will give the half-backs and three-quarters more opportunities of working in combination.

Another important ruling is that "when a player accidentally knocks-on or throws the ball forward, and he or one of the opposing side obtains possession of it before it falls to the ground, such knock-on or throw forward shall be exempted from the penalty for acci- dental knook-on in this by-law." How often in the Past have we all had to deplore the absence of some such law. Trifling knocks onin catching have spoiled scores Of the best passing runs, while many a man has been unable to profit from a clear opening presented him by an opponent who has thrown forward accidentally. By the new rule a very bad pass forward may be turned to excellent account by theNother side, and play generally should be brightened up

The General Committee met afterwards and made an important change regarding the cup-ties. February 14th and 21st, March 7th and 21st, April 4th and 25th were selected as cup-tie dates for the coming season,and it was also decided that the draw should take place at the conclusion of each round. It is hoped that even greater interest will be created by this means, but it is questionable whether the majority of people will wel- come the. change. There was a certain amount of pleasure in knowing beforehand whom you were likely to meet, spectators in particular being thus enabled to make arrangements for seeing matches, which they will not new be able to anticipate. However "time will i tell," and there s no harm in the committee trying the experiment of drawing "fresh after each round. It is just possible that the interest of the crowd may be iurther stimulated by this means.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

The members of the Royal Cycling Club took part in a "paper chase "on Saturday. Messrs H Gerrard, A Wright, and W H Robinson, jun., started at 2.30 from Walton New-road to act as hares and lay the trail. w H Robinson was mounted on his motor "bike " carry- ing the scent. The hounds, viz., the remainder of the club, took up the chase at 2.45, proceeding along the trail to Frodsham and thence to Kingsley, where some

a the hounds gave up the chase and played bowls at the Horse Shoe. The more tenacious of the hounds hung on as far as Crowton where they lost the scent. Here the hounds spread out, and after some searching ' found the trail again, and with a" Tally-Ho" went on with redoubled vigour on the track of the hares as far as Acton Bridge. Here the hares had exercised con- siderable ingenuity in doubling back on their trail, and the hounds were put to some trouble and much fun in picking up the trail, which they found just in time to prevent several young rustics from picking up and put- ting on another track. From Acton Bridge they went to Weaverham Bridge, and thence to Stretton. Here the scent was hot, and the hounds eager, and with a final dash of two miles the hares were run down on London Bridge with the following result :-1, Bert Powell; 2, C A Gornall ; 3, H Davenport—one length, half a wheel. In the hill-climbing contest the results were as follows : 1, J A Watson ; 2, C E Hatton ; and 3, G H Anderton.

Foot Racing. At the Broughton Harriers Sports, E Harris, of the Warrington A.C. won the first prize in the quarter mile open handicap, and C J Straw, a member of the same club won the one mile handicap, being conceded a start of 100 yards.

Personal. Lady Stamford and Warrington has left Bill- street. London, for Bradgate Park, Leicestershire. r3e old house at Brarlgate, now an ivy-clad ruin, was (the " World "remarks) the birthplace of Lady Jane Grey, The new hove is a modern Elizabethan building. The park, which is really a section of Charnwood Forest, is very picture=que and well timbered. There are some remarkably fine oaks and Spanish chestnuts. Groby Mese,a beautiful lake of forty acres, is a great resort of wildfowl, in the time of the late Lord Stamford the estate of Brad- gate was one of the best sporting domains in Eng- I land. Mr Adrian Hope ranted the place for somel years. The Bradgate prope-ty which is a large one, belongs to Lady Stamford and Warrington for her life, and passes asterwarda to Mr Arthur Dun- e. Warring-ton Musical Society. The annual reports of the past season in connec- tion with the Warrington Musical Society are now in the hands of the members and they will be sub- mitted for confirmation on Tuesday evening next when the annual general meeting 11l be held in Trinity schoolroom. The hon. secretaries (Messrs W E Atkin and 1' J Lord) in their report state that the attendance of members at rehearsals and con- certs was on the whole good, but again a falling off in numbers towards the end of the season, after Christmas, had to be noted with regret. The numerical strength of the chorus was 154 or 16 less than in the 19004 I season, and the orohestrs nambere 1 33 instrumen- talists being a decrease of 1. The number of sub- scribers to the concerts (137 names on the books) had not decreased, but the sale of tickets to non- subscribers fell off considerably. "The committee feel the difficulty" continues the report," of secur- ing a general support from the public to be very great indeed, and the popularizing of the concerts without deteriorating the standard and class of programme is each year a problem which becomes harder and harder to solve." The Conductor is congratulated in the report on having attended all the rehearsals but one, f mm which, unfortunately, illness prevented his attend- ance. The dance in aid of the funds resulted in a net profit of just over £5O. The secretaries con- clude the report by stating that " the Committee has received with great regret and most unwillingly felt bound to accept the resignation by kr G F F White, of his post as hon. librarian. The sincerest thanks of the Society are due to him for his invalu- able service in this connection during several years."—Mr L W Reynolds, the hon. treasurer, sub- mits his financial statement, from which it appears that there was a loss on the season's work of £3l lit 4d, Fortunately the proceeds of the dance more than cover this loss, and the deficiency on previous accounts has been reduced from £154 Os 3d to £139 5s Id.

A gentleman named Bruce Brawn, of Dunoon, Scot- land, died on Wednesday at °smotherley, a Yorkshire village, as the result of a cycling .accideat. He was spending his honeymoon at Stockton-on-Tees, and on Saturday, whilst cycling with his wife on Osinetharley moor,. lost control of his machine on a steep hill, and was picked up at the bottom shuckingly injured.

Rev H A Lester, Rev G V and Mrs Owen, Bey B and Mrs Percival, Rev W and Mrs Pollock-Hill, Rev F E Powell, Rev A N Taylor, Rev D Kerrin,RevJ Bell Cox,Rev E J and Mrs Willcocks. THE PRINCIPAL'S SPEECH.

The Rev. MOR—LE-Y STEVENSON, in reviewing the year's work, said the result of the examinations had been uiliformly good, and without wearying the audience I with statistice or figuree they might take it from him ' that they vzoreentirely eateified with the remits of their I work. The report of his Majesty's Inspector of Training I Colleges, Mr W Scott Coward, of the Sete June, stated ' that—" The college is admirably coadocted on broad ' lines and in the freest spirit, The students are in excel- lent ord-r, and are hippy in their college life and sullies. Their reading and recitation (including the 1 French exercise) deserve much praise." If it had not been for those who worked with him such results could I not have been produced, and he owed it to them as well AS to himself to say publicly, as he rejoined to do, what a deep debt of gratitude he n wed to his fellow-workers, and how well they had tried to carry out all he I had inspired them with. The result was that their work had been blessed ant had succeeded. The future of training colleges, to pass from their own was a very serious oue. Ho wanted to mention two things The first wee thit training colleges were diverg- ing into two kin:l,3—d Ls, colleges in which the students did not reside, and the residential colleges. It might be a question in tho future which of Haase two kinds of colleges was going to be the future college of the COOK- try ; and looking at the matter quite dispassionately there was something to be said on both sides. It was not for him to dogmatize or lay down a law and say that one was better than the other, but as one who bad over 20 years' experience in residential celleges he should like to say that he believed there were advent- ' ages in residential colleges which it would be unwise for the country to ignore. The common and corporate life ' of the students, the knitting together of friendships, the rubbing one againse another, the social life of a ' college, with all its social pleasures and iratel- ' lecteal gains, were not things to be lightly cast aside. To young man or young woman who live I in lodgings, or in his or her own home, and Game to town by tram and attended c ertain lectures and went home again derived great benefit, but not the same kind as the yeung man or ya ine woman who lived the corporate life in a well-ordered institution; and he was sure that the constant contact with those who were older and better educated, and with those who were constantly thinking about everything which might minister to the greater culture, the greater refinement,- the greater intellootual life, and above all, the moral development of the students, was an advantage which could hardly be over-estimated. (Applause.) Whatever might be the future, he hoped the day and residential colleges might be allowed to run on parallel lines side by side, that each might learn something from the other, as each could, but thet they would in no hasty spirit overthrow the old system of the residential college arid replace it too hastily by a now and less tried plan (Applause.) The other point was this —There had been a vary warm debate in the House of Commons that week over ,14 the question of denomina- tionsi colleges, and it wae evident there was a strong feeling in the minds of many that the denominational colleges ought to have what was commonly called " the conscience clause," and to be thrown open to everyone. fie said this in no spirit of narrowness. He was no foe to his Noncon- formist friends ; on the contrary he had many dear Non- e-info:mist friends. Nor was he opposed at all to all Nonconformist teachers having every possible gain and advantage they could have, but these who:talked of in- troducing a conscienoo clause intol a residential college did not quite understand-what it meant.lt was said"We have intreduced the conscience clause into the day school, why not hato the training college ?"—for this reason, that the one was a day school and the other a residential one. When they had people living together like one family, attending the Same service and ehepel, receiving the same teaching, they wanted above all things to keep the whole household in a state ef unity, but the introduction into that household of those who had been nurtured in a different feral of faith was a very awkward el iment to deal with. It would be a deep regret to him to feel that any student of his was unable to keel side by side with her fellow-student and worship God in her own college chapel, and to feel, as was advocated in the twine of Commons that week, that when Sunday morning came one might go to one place of worship and another to another, not becalm, he did not respect the conscientious convictions , which would lead them te do so, hut because he felt that the corporate life of the college and the unity of spirit in which they nould all join together to worship one God was lost. (Applause). But some said there was a genuine grievance as the Nonconformist teacher could not I get into colleges. That had been grossly exaggerated, and he could not understand the figures quoted in the House of Commons. In the debate on the second reading of the Education Bill one gentleman said there were only two undenominational colleges in England. In one sense of the word it was true. There were only two which had that particular labeebut be had left out of sight that there were several colleges which were undenominational and several day 'colleges which i took no cognizance of religion at all; in fact there were no fewer than 28 colleges in the kingdom open to Noncon- formists, and there were 31 Church of England colleges. When they considered that the number of Church people was greater than the number of Nonconformists it would be seen that the proportion was a very fair' one. The idea that there was any reel grievance or difficulty in the Nonconformist teacher being able In enter the train- ing cell ge was a difficulty which he granted existed years ego, but it no longer existed. What happened was this : There were colleges which were special favour- ites, sad into these everyone wished to press. They could not all get in, and having failed to get in they were, perhaps, unable to get in elsewhere because other colleges had filled up the list ; but, take the colleges throughout the country, number by number,they would find there was sufficient accommodation for Noncon- formist teachers equally with Church teachers, and just as many Church teachers were dieappeinted of entrance into the training colleges every year as Nonconformist teachers, and probably more. Perhaps these were poli- tical matters to introduce, but when they read these things in the newspapers they should remember that there was a great deal to be said en the side of the residential college and the Church college. He booed it would be very long before they parted lightly with an institution which, without the slightest doubt, had been of incalculable service to the Country. (Applause). Sir EDWARD RUSSELL, who Was cordiality received, said he might be excused if for a single moment he justified and explained his personal position. He was, as they 1 all knew, no expert in educational matters. Ho was not officially or professionally responsible for, nor com- petent to deal with any church matters. But they also perhaps knew that he could claim in the ordinary course of his life to be a sort of representative for the outside world, and knew pretty well what the outside world was saying, and so combination of rather special interests in such subjects had brought them together that day. He believed that if there were lese talking about educa- tion and more doing of it—more avoidance of subject's which hampered education, and that prevented agree- ment upon it—they would get on a great deal better. (Hear, hear.) It was a pleasure to leim—it personal pleasure—to find himself there, near an old friend of his, the Dean of Manchester,who was connected effisielly with that college, and who not only showed there, but
Progn

letd exhibited in his owa eity, what rs,ct and persona magnetism and assiduity in the good cause of edulation could do under circumstances which were honestly sup- posed to be of great difficulty—to make the education of the people efficient,andeto encourage everything which made for that efficiency, and also to avoid to the ut- most extent the difficulties by which popular education was supposed to be surrounded. (Applause.) They at that college were doing the same thing in their own way, and a vary pleasant way it WIC He must say that a place more fraught with evidences of pleasant- ness of life to persons going through part of their educ t- tion, which had been afforded to him by his delightsd inspection of the place, Gould not possibly be had. He was sure that there the young ladies, who were at a period in the very bloom and promise of their early life as women, trainine themselves for the great businees of their careers—he was sure it was a delightful thing to be convinced teat they were doing it con emote,, with a thorough feeling of the irnportattee of it. It was a gratification to know it,and to feel that every- one who entered ipon the scholastic business went through the place and came out of it stronger and more cheerful because of the life they had led there. eees to the points the Principal bad treated with so mien dii- cretion, although he would net attempt to pronounce 1 upeu the question between resident and day collegesnie thought that they tnight at any rate accept his cenelu- sinus. Colleges ought not to be put an end to where they were doing good, and they ought not to be die- turbed where the disturbance would lessen the gaol they were doing, and both sorts of colleges , oueht to be allowed to go on concurrently and ' co-operatively in the good work they were doing. Let them vaeue anything that was really and truly to the evidence of their observation and criticism doing good, and let the last thing of which they ware con- vinced be that that good ought to be disturbed, and that such colleges should he put an end to. Teen', he was convinced, the course was thoroughly pleasant to those who came. There they were all happy and cheery. Teey were being equipped for the good work which they would have to do, aid the great delight or their equipment would eeoeiet, in toe long run, in the intellectual interests which had been excited in them in that college (Applause). they were doing those duties in that manner, and enjoying their pursuits in that manner, as a preparation for their subsequent life. In the first place, they were preparing to get their living in one of the noblest avocation i—an avocation universallte respected —an avocation in which success was greatly admired and he whioh it might also be said that the pore mal traits which contributed to the success and the personal :peculiarities which made for success, were always most cordially peel admiringly recognised in these who had them. (Applause). Tuey Looked forward to the privilege and the advantage of enabling others to get their living in this world, and that thought should give a subitantial setisfactioe to every teacher .of young people. They would be chiefle engaged in teaching girls, and the position of industrial lifewas such that up to now, although greatly extended, it still was a matter of considerable uncertainty and wouldtheTa subject of very great development in the future. They were teaching many also who weuld have to get their living in the way in which it was an advan- tage that most women should earn their living, and no happiness so won could be better deserved. Be meant ths gathering, the managing, the consolidating, and the gladdening of the home. (Applause). Tney would be sisters, housekeepers, and wives, and through- out the whole of their life the life they lived would be more or less a power, nitre or ICES an advanttge, more or less a facility, in dir-ctine the happiness of mankind in proportion as these young ladies were able to teach them, in proportion as they were able to profit by th • teaching of those e oung, lives. The studies there would provide for the leisure of those who were now students. They would provide them with resources throdgh life to give them a constant satisfaction. They would find he was co evineeel, if they took a serious view of life, and at eheZsame time to ik a bright and cheerful view of life they would find that the brigeter, higher, and more genial life was to be the reeult of education even more than of the mere bresd-winnieg side of life, in the creation of an intellectual appetite, everything made for a healthy and pleasant occupation of the human mind. Take, for instance, the very ordinary case of reading. There were, perhaps, three classes in the ordinary life of people—so ee who did not read as, all, 'erne who only reed newsomers—(laughter),—and some who also read books. That was a distinct rising from one stage to another, and the highest stsp was perfectly attainable by persons in ordinary posi- tion!' of life, and the result at any rate of attaining that spirit, where there was a real earnest appetite, would be a better life in the home, however hutrib'e that home might be. Let them ask for a moment what I was the difference in homes. He thought that if they took an English home ; what made the most practical difference in the homes of this country was temperance. 'And in the next importance was temper; and they might 1 say next of importance was refinement. All those things were the result of cultivation. They had a great oppor- tunity of study, not only the study of books, but the study of character. There were different faculties, qualities, and characteristics to study. It was a most satisfactory thing that in the whole turmoil in which they had been living in educaienal matters it had been universally regegnisea that there was a great necessity for training colleges, and that the teachers should be trained for their work. Their powers should be brought out by two sides which might a'nsoet seem in opposi- tion to each other, but which were not. It was vary necessary that a teacher should have and acquire the knack of instruction because with alt che knowledge and instruction in the world they could not educate without the knack of teaching. In the second place, it was necessary that it should not be all knack. There was a good deal of surface.work in that metter,and because people bad an apparent practice and facility of producing their effect upon the class and upon the schools they should take care that the facility got in instruction should also be sup- ported by the soundest knowledge and m tat capable in - struction. There was only one other point upon which he would trouble them with any remirks. He did not for- get that that was a Church of England College, and he did not forget that questions connected with the Church of England were at most times thorny, and at the present time exceedingly thorny. He would like to be permitted in a very few words to claim the right of the people of this country to have in the clergy of the country, and in those who were noncerrieliri the Church of England education of the people of this country, ono thing. and that was moderation of their Churchmanship. The education of this country would have been very different if that doctrine bad always been observed. In all Church matters, and especially in dealing with the State or with public affairs, it should be a point of honour to adher3 to the moderation of the Church ' • and thisewould prove a point of policy also, for it would make for the perpetuity of the Church's power, in education as in everything. They should be as moderate as passible in the expression and in the main- tenanee of their church views. He was convinced that it was not only a point of honour, but a point of policy; and if observed conscientiously and courteously by all persona it would be greatly to the advantage of Church of England eduo•tion and to the best advantage for the future of the race.
