NORTHERN UNION.
Annual General Meeting. Some Interesting Decisions.

The annual meeting of the Union was held on Tuesday night at the George Hotel, Huddersfield, Mr d Clifford. in the absence of Mr J H Houghton, the president, in the chair. Thera was not so large on attendance of the club represeatatioes as usual. The report and balance-sheet were taken as read, and they were adopted without discussion.

div.head: PUNT-OUT ABOLISHED.
div.p: PUNT-OUT ABOLISHED.

Mr Smith proposed to delete law 12. and substitute the following: "The ball is in touch when it or a play r carry- ing it tonah or cross the touch line • it shall then be taken into play ten yards from and at right angles to the touch line, and there put down and serurnmaged." This was the most im portent alteration they bad to propose. Five years ago they were not satisfied with the play resulting from the throw out from touoh, which although thought to be a perfect method of bringing the ball into play did not work out so, and thee thought that the pant out would do away with the disad- vantages. He had beea a strong advosate of the punt out, and they hoped players would valize the possibilities of the punt out, but he was not sure that the players bad realised them, and that not having so don the committ es though-, it Was necessary to try something else. There was us doubt that sooner or later the punt out rule would have to be abolished. The substitution of the scrummage was thought to be the best course that could be adopted, and he hoped that the proposed alteration would be wiled. Mr Charlesworth (Dewsbury) seconded the resolution. Mr J Platt said It was absolutely necsssary to make the alteration. The game had not progressed since the present , law was intro lucel, and the rule had entirely killed centre three-quarter play. and there was not the same quality of centre three-quarters ss there was before the intro suction of the rule. He thought they ought to play scientific football and to take away as much danger as possible. The punt out was neither nice nor scientific. and he thought that they would :save time by making the proposed alteration. A centre three-quarter who had done great service in the past had told him that he had not played a cool centre three- quarter game since the rule had been altered. Mr Lister, Bradford, supported the alteration. Mr Worthington, Swinton, opposed on the grounds that the alteration would develop a tendency to kick into touch again and waste time. Mr Cooke, Wakefield. eu, ported the alteration, and the vote was then taken : For the Change, 42; against, 9. (Applause) The following alterations were agreed to without discus- sloe:— Law 2—Delete the words A neutral touch judir, in ad- dition to holding up his flag when and where the bill goes Into touch shall decide to which side the ball belongs."

Law 13—After last portion of rule to read as fellows :—"ln case a player when running with the ball ',trusses his oppo- nents gnU line and then touches the referes or touch-judge, he shall be allowed a try where such official was touched. When a player. running out from his own in-goal, touches the referee or touch.j adge the bill is dead at the spot where such official is touched, to". Law lg.—Delete last par and substitute as follows : " Whenla player accidentally knocks or throws the bail for- word, and he or one of the opposing side obtains possession before it falls to the ground, such knock-on or throw forward shall be exempted from the penalty for accidental knock-on I In this by-law." div.head: Meeting of the Committee.

Dates of the Cup Ties.
In the coarse of the afternoon the General Committee of the NJrthern Union held a meeting. Mr 7 Clifford, of Huddersfield in the:chair. The attendanee was a representa- tive one.
CIIP TIE DATES: IMPORTANT CHANGE IN THE DRAW; The Committee decided that the Cup Tie dated! for the ensuing season should be as follows : February 14th, February 21. March 7th, March 21st. _ _

April 4th, 'April 25th. It was agreed that the draw should take place at the con- clusion of each round, the object being to create a greater amount of interest in the tournament than is possible now, when the draw is so arranged that clubs can tell upon which ground a given match is played in certain eventualities.

- A NOTEL SITUATION, The Goole Club reported that the Radcliffe Club had agaia failed to pay them their share of the gate in connection with the First Round of the Cup-Ties, and asked the Committee to take action at law on their behalf for the recovery of the money. The Committee decided that they could not take action themselves, but promised that if the Goole Club took proaeediegs. they would be prepared to Support them In tho matter of law costs.

Recent circumstances have made ournahstre prophets very shy of forecasting actual days and dates ; but at the time of writing it is confidently hoped that, by the time of publication,Lord Kitchener will once more be back in England after nearly two years and a half at the front. One thing, how- ever, is certain, that his reception will be flu- parallelled in the history of modern triumphs, unless unforeseen events occur to prevent the demonstration with which his grateful and en- thusiastic fellow-countrymen are bubbling over. When Lord Roberts left Pretoria amidst a fanfare of trumpets, he 16ft behind him such a legac7 as would appal the boldest; but his second-m-command quitely set to work to fight by far the more trying part of the War. Amidst grumbling and discontent he laid his far reaching plans and calmly laboured, regardless of criticism, to break the back of the opposition as surely as it had to be slowly; and by months and months of unostentatious work, gradually the blockhouse system was com- pleted, and little by little the Boers found themselves hedged in on all sides, till opposition was hopeless. The consistency of his conduct, the modesty of his demeanour and despatches, his unflinching determination coupled with his broad- mindedness, have combined to make him to-day the most popular man in the Empire, and the nation's hero and idol, in addition to which he holds the unique position of being both our chief war-wager and our leading peacemaker. South- ampton. by geographical good luck, has the first chance of welcoming him and adding him to its distinguished list of freemen, after which he travels on to town, arriving at Paddington, where he is toi be met by the Prince of Wales, the Commander-in- Chief, and many of the most prominent men in the Empire, and escorted in triumph through the
EVENTS OF THE WEEK ILLUSTRATED.
SIR JOHN FRENCH, 1C.C.8.

streets or London by detachments of Indian Lid Colonial troops, as well as regulars. Had Hit Majesty only been in good health he would nu. doubtedly have met him in person, and the luncheon would have taken place at Buckingham Palace in- stead of the War Office, but under the present sad circumstances it is of course impossible, though perhaps he may be well enough to receive Lord Kitchener a few minutes later in the day, and the Queen will probably take a prominent part in the reception. Anyhow, the warmth of the Empire's greeting is as well assured as it has been well earned. Bene meruit de patrine, the highest praise the Romans ever gave. Two other generals, both of whom stand high in popularity, arrive this week Lord Methuen, who has worked nn- flaggingly, and is more truly beloved by the men under him than any other of our com- manding officers, and Sir John French. who has a proud record to look back on, and has won himself a great name amidst the grave of many reputations. Their advent may be over- shadowed by the presence of their Commander-in- Chief, but it will not be overlooked or forgotten. Generals Bruce Hamilton and Eliot, who ase also to be reckoned amongst those who have won great laurels in South Africa, will soon be home, as they have already sailed; and the War Office have issued a statement showing the order in which the troops will be sent back and disbanded. 'The first 70.000 will consist of (i) Volunteers 2,500, and Colonial troops 7,500; (ii) Militia, 4,000; Yeoraany, 8,000; and (iv) Reservists 50,000; and after them will come the militia despatched this year, 12,000; and the Regulars in settled order, all coming home as soon as possible. except as many as are deemed necessary for the purpose of settling the country nd tho 3 e on the roster for foreign service.

In connection with the disastrous postponement af the Coronation and hi 9 Majesty's dangerous illness, one event will always be remembered, and that is, the highly successful dinner to which, despite his own condition, the King •entertained half a million of his poorest subjects. One of the first official announcements in connection with the Coronation was that King Edward had set wide £30,000 out of his privy purse for the purpose of providing a banquet for those of his people who would be least likely to participate in the general rejoicings and festivities of the time. Hence, last Saturday, all went off without a hitch. except for the enforced absence of the royal host. His place, however, was as far as possible filled by the Prince and Princess of Wales. who visited the dinners in the gardens of Fulham Palace, Victoria Park, and elsewhere, while others were honoured by the presence of the Duchess of r?ife, the Duchess of Argyll, and other leading members of the Royal Family acting as deputies. The dinners were held simultaneously in various public parks, halls, and other places lent for the occasion, and consisted of liberal supplies of beef, lamb, potatoes, fruit pies, cheese and many "etceteras," including beer, mineral waters, and tobacco. The King's guests, who were all presented with a mug in commemo• ration of the happy day, were dressed in their best
THE BoIIVENIE CUP.
THE PRINCE OP' WALES VISITING THE NINO'S DINNER AT FULHAM. _ _

in honour of the occasion; and it was obvious that all enjoyed themselves immensely. Messrs. 11. E. Moss, Adney Payne, Philip Yorke, and others combined in organising entertainments to follow the dinners, and many of the leading "stars" generously gave their services, which were heartily applauded. Her Majesty has also been entertaining this week, and will continue to do so during next at various selected centres. Her guests are ten thousand maid-servants from all parts of London. who are taking tea with the Queen, and they likewise have been presented with a souvenir in the shape of a chocolate-box. It is difficult to assess how greatly these kind and thoughtful acts of King Edward and Queen Alexandra have increased their already immense popularity, especially under the circumstances. The conference of the Colonial Premiers, which is at present in session at the Colonial Office under the presidency of Mr. Chamberlain in his capacity of Secretary of State for the Colonies, thongh held in camerel, is exciting great general interest, and it is thought that some important results may accrue from this skilfully devised meeting of the leading representatives of the Colonies, who are consulting and being consulted by many of the leading men ot the Mother Country. The Conference consists of the Colonial Secretary, as noted above, Sir Wilfred Laurier (Canada), Sir Edmund Barton (Australia), the Rt. Hon. Richard Seddon (New Zealand), Sir J. Gordon Sprigg (Cape Colony), Sir Albert Hime (Natal), Sir Robert Bond '(Newfoundland), Lord Onslow (the Under-Secretary for the Colonies), Sir M. Ommaney (the Permanent Under-Secretary, and Sir J. Anderson (Secretary). It has met at intervals during the past ten days, and will continue to do so for the next week, and many important Imperial problems are being thrashed out at this fortunate foregathering of representatives. One drawback only exists-,—that none, except Mr. Seddon, are vested with plenipotentiary powers,so that all matters will have to be referred to the respective parliaments, except' in a few instances, such as the case of Canada and subsidies, when standing statutes authorise negotiations. The principal questions under discussion are general political relations, the matter of Imperial defence, inter-communication, naturalisation, Colonial legal anocedure, and the Pacific Islands, and the Australasian Colonies, most of which subjects embrace many sub-proposals, while it is expected -that ;Progress will be made in the arrangement of triennial

sonforenees for joint deliberation, the organisation of lan I and sea forces in the Colonies, and the im- portant and debatable question of preferential rates. From this outline it may be gathered that th.
THE COLONIAL PREMIERS' CONFERENCE.
7, RT. HON. JOSESSE CHAMBERLAIN. 2, RT. HON SIR WILFRED LAURIER. 3, RT. HON. E. BARTON. 4, RT. HON. R. J. SEBDoIi. 5, RT. HON. SIR GORDON SPRIGG. 6, RT,, HON. SIR H. A. RIME. 7, RT. HON. ROBERT BOND.

conference is one of no little importance and may do much to consolidate the various interests of the Empire into one united whole. Meanwhile,the Colonial Premiers have been having a right roytil time, and will go away with a good idea of British hospitality.

Henley is always a pleasant function and now- a-days is only second in social popularity to Ascot. Time was not so very long ago when this most important of the Thames regattas attracted only rowing men and habitues of the river for the most part, but of late years it has each summer become more generally regarded as a pleasant relaxation in the London season and a fashionable meeting- place for society. This year its popularity was more marked than ever, as. although there was a falling off of entries, the racing was even more interesting than usual, as it was not only inter- national in character, but also included entries from the Colonies. One new feature of the arrangements was the renting of Phyllis Court, the residence of the late Mr. Hugh Mair, by the stewards of the meeting to serve as a regatta. enclosure, and its spacious lawn, adjoining the

div.head: 'SICIAN
div.p: 'SICIAN

SNAP-SHOTS AT HENLEY. winning-post, afforded a particularly pleasant promenade under the grand old elms, combined with an exceptionally excellent view of the racing. There were marquees for lunch and tea, and the band of the "Queen's Bays" greatly added to the attractiveness each afternoon. In front of Phyllis Court were ranged seven launches, and below the Isthmian Club enclosure, in Section 1, came the houseboats of the London Rowing Club, Balliol College, Christchurch, Sir T. Dewar' s Fair' Maid of Perth, and many other splendid floatingd houses, while below Fawley Court .the line-extend ed almost to the starting point. In-every -detail the regatta was a great credit to the stewards;mnd, one of the best organised which has ever taken place.

EVEN in his staunchest The Right Decision. Radical days Mr °HAM- A:a BERLAIN (whose health let us hope, will not really suffer from his unfor- tunate accident) could have reached no sounder decision than he has taken in the case of the Cape Constitution. Liberals will not be chary in their praise, the more so because it can have been no easy feat to break with Lord Mils Ea and the Rhodesian clique, not to speak of their docile organs in this country,:frona the " Times " down- wards. It is possible to-day to take a bright view of the prospects of a real settlement in South Africa. The declaration of peace did much, but it is hardly an exaggeration to say that the suspen- sion of the Cape Constitution would have jeopard- ised everything which the treaty seemed to secure. Had we followed Lord MILNER'S advice, and inaugurated the new era ioy establishing a despotism in Cape Colony,we should have aroused a degree of mistrust and discontent which would have undermined very swiftly indeed the good feeling that had begun to make itself felt. It was only one section of one race in Cape Colony—the extreme party which took its lead from Mr. RHODES and Dr. JAM ESON—which had clamoured for this violent intervention. They professed, indeed, that their object was to avoid the unrest which might have followed a meeting of the Cape Parliament. In reality their proposal was the° the government of the Colony should be handed over to a little council of their own nominees, which was to have the power to administer the country and to rearrange the constituencies so as Ito secure them a majority at the next election. No sane man could possible imagine that such an arrangement would be conducive to contentment. Neither the Liberal Eoglish section, to which the whole of the present Cape Ministry belongs,nor the Dutch colonists would have tamely submitted to a despotism of this type. Nor would the indignation have been confined to the Cape. The Boers of the late Republics would have made common cause with their kinsmen, and everywhere the idea that South Africans must unite to resist the meddle- some interference of Downing-street would have gained ground. But that danger, we may hope, has passed, and there is now every prospect that the sober minds of both parties will come together to found a strong yet loyal party for the defence of their constitutional liberties, not against the Imperial Government which respects them, but against the corrupt financial ring which organised first the Jameson invasion of 1895, then the war, and now this impudent raid on the liberties of Cape Colony. As for Lord MILNER, who so far forgot his vosition of civil servant as to make him- self the mouthpiece of this movement, it is to be hoped that this rebuff may hasten his resignation. If he should, however, choose to cling to his post it will be with diminished prestige and lessened power.
THE deliberations of the Cross-Purposes. Colonial Premiers, who sit

ClOStted with Mr. CHAMBER' LAIN for several days in the week, are likely to re- main for some time a profound secret. But a meeting of the British Empire League the other day set ved to show clearly enough the issues that really divide the two parties to the federation which the COLONIAL SECRETARY is striving to bring about. The Doss of DEVONSHIRE spoke for this country, Sir E. BARTON and Sir G. SPRIGO for the Colonies. They all taiked more or less in parables, but it was tolerably obvious that :all the while they were reading solemn lectures to one another. The Doan of DEVONSHIRE on one point at least spoke boldly and distinctly. Our paramount duty, he said, was to arrange for some scheme of , Imperial defence, This, he declared, was the royal road to federation. It was, moreover, a pressing matter which brooked no delay, and if we procrastinated we should awake some day to find that we had no longer an Empire to defend. This may sound innocent enough, but consider the facts. Imperial Defence is the one subject which the larger colonies have bluntly refused to discuss. Australia is passing through a financial crisis so grave that she has had to lower the salary of her Governor and to cut down the modest estimates for local defence. She was never less likely to think of contributing to our Navy, still less to our Army. Canada has been very explicit also. Sir W. LAURIER has told Us that she does not mean to be drawn into the vor- tex of European militarism. During the war no doubt the Colonies did much for us. But they sent men only—it was we who paid them. If that is the limit of Colonial tinthusiasrn IR time of ;war and excitement, it seems useless to look for more in time of peace. But sooner had the Duke sat down with this weighty utterance than the various Colonial magnates rose up one after another with a proposal no less

impossible. About Imperial Defence they were politely silent. The key to Imperial Federation, in their view, lay in preferential trade. We must abandon our prejudices, drop Free Trade, and give their imports a preference over those of foreign countries. But it is only a fortnight since the CHANCELLOR of the EXCEQUER declared in the name of the Government that we could not pos- sibly consider any sweeping seleme of that des- cription. The Bread Tax is sufficiently unpopular. It is clear that no Ministry dare impose similar duties on meat and wool and timber for the benefit of the Colonies which produce them. Where, then, is the common ground between our own Imperialists and the Colonies? We will not tax ourselves to foster their industries. They will not tax themselves to maintain our armaments. The Conference, it seems clear, is playing at cross- purposes.
THE old days of

The Evictions Begin. Coercion and Eviction have come once more to Ireland. If, as we all hope, the Coronation will be celebrated in a few weeks' time, it will find the land war in its most embittered stages, a British Minister employing British bayonets to drive a few hundreds of desperat3 peasants from their miserable huts at the bidding of a clique of land- lords. The process has begun already on the De Freyne estate. No one who knows anything of the facts can fail to pity these wretched people, and to admit the justice of their cause. The facts ought to be known to every elector, and, at the risk of repetition, it would be well to state them once more. The Dillon and the De Freyue estates in Mayo and Roscommon lie side by side, the soil of both equally poor, the peasants of both con- triving to subsist rather on what thdir sons make as harvesters in Great Britain, or their daughters as servant, girls in America, that on anything they can wring from the half-drained bog or the stony hillside. They live on maize, and the family income ranges from £7 to £3O a year. Recently, taking pity on their case, the Congested Districts Board stepped in and bought the Dillon property. Its first act was to wipe off £2,0,000 of arrears, and to lower the rents by 33 per cent. Rents, however, they are no longer, but Purchase instalments, and in duo course every peasant or his son will own his own plot of land. Naturally the De*Freyne tenants aske.i for equal treatment. Lord DE FREYNE was unwilling. Agitation followed, and the Givernment then de- clared that since these poor people had clamoured for justice they must wait. Then the tenants formed a combination, and suggested as a com-

Promise a reduction of 15 per cent. in their rents. Still Lord Dz FREYNE refused. And now the in- evitable is happening—evictions, and all the entail. How long shall we think it necessary to support the injustice by force, and to pledge the support of the Empire to the hardest race of land- lords who ever extorted an unearned rent from a starving peasantry? There will be no hope for this wretched countr3 until Liberals face this question courageously, and ask themselves seriously why Irishmen alone in all the Empire are disloyal and aloof in this year of Coronation and Peace.

The discussion on the Foreign Office Vote not a very exciting event, for the simple re that the Government's case was presented by Lord Cranborne, a gentleman whose only claim to the position he holds is that he happens to have come into the world as Lord Salisbury's eldest son. He had no intelligent defence to offer of the carious apathy which has allowed us to lose the alliance of Italy, our traditional friend, of whose co-opera- tion in the Nlediterranean we were, until recently, assured. By our blundering,first in the Armenian business, when Signor Crisp' mobilised an army to assist our fleet which never sailed on its crusade of rescue; then in the afiir of the Tripolitan hinterland ; and lastly by Mr Cl amberlain's obstinacy in attempting to crush ths Italian lan- guage in Malta, we have driven Italy into the arms of France. Again to the question why we have followed Germany rather than the United States, in a vindictive policy against China, Lord Cranborne could only answer that he was sure China realised that we were her best friend. But the climax came when in speaking of Japan, he arrogantly declared, "We\ do not seek treaties— eve grant them." A diplomat who goes out of his way in this fashion to insult our few remaining friends in order to raise a Jingo cheer proves him- self not merely incompetent but mischievous.

Just now, while deputations and their cost are interesting items to the ratepayers, it may be well to contrast the systems of two of our local autho- rities. The Warrington Town Council sends aumerous deputations and pays for them out of the public funds, while the Warrington Rural bistrict is content with very few, and the mem- bers pay the cost out of their own pockets. Oovernment auditors are apt to be severe on the question of deputation expenses, and the Rural Councillors, rather than risk a rebufl,take the very Praiseworthy course of paying for themselves when they are out for the day on Council business. Their deputations, moreover, have none of the attractions that a visit to the Clio possesses. They are purely business affairs, taking up a consider- able amount of time and making a by no means in- significant call on the pockets of the members. All honour to the Rural Councillors They attend faithfully to their humdrum duties without expect- ing any reward such as an annual picnic at the expense of their constituents. The Warrington Borough Treasurer has issued a portly tome of over 200 pages containing au ab. stract of the accounts of the Corporation for the year ended 31st March, 1902. It contains a mass of statistics relative to the numerous Corporation departments, which should prove more than a littleinteresting to watchful ratepayers. Tha aggregate balance statement shows a bal- ance of assets. i over liabilities amounting to £317,333. T i ins s far more satisfactory than many anticipated and s .pleasanter reading than the return of the rates levied in the borough', Which shows that the avorage rates for the past eix years are scl in the pound higher than in the 12receding ten years, when the . average was only ;In 9d in the pound. Deficiencies are shown on the elecricity and tramways departments but no alls upon the rates have yet been made them. Ratepayers are looking forward to these new undertakings becoming profitable ,'ventures and affording some relief to the rates. dndging from the published returns the prospect not seem of the brightest, but there is a To- ning fact that both departments are progressing, the next balance sheets may be distinctly gratifying. It must not be forgotten that the el .ectricity and tramways undertakings are muni- e'Pal infants—and infants with a promising future.

a,The Local GL.vernment Board have saved the `listrict from the threatened nuisance in connec- Icsith the Winwick Asylum Sewage Scheme. The 12,pard has very properly declined the application the Asylums Board to sanction the loan of ;1"3,000 for connecting the Winwick Asylum drain `.;.?. the sewer belonging to the Warrington Rural t'Strict Council and for extending that sewer to t ellara Brook, on the ground that it was proposed turn the sewage into the brook without treat- over land. The derision will be welcomed 0? all the inhabitants who live in the vicinity 4nkey Brook. The proposal of the Asylums —oar th El was a retrograde one and well deserved e fate which has befallen it. The decision of

' the Local Government Board has already used the Committee of Visitors tor Winwick Asylum to ; devise a more scientific means of dealing with the I sewage. At a special meeting of the Board held lon Thursday it was decided to expend £4,000 on la scheme for dealing with the sewage on the ' bacteriological system. Tbis is certainly a more desirable way of solving the sewage difficulty and it is a matter for surprise that the Board did not I propose this s3heme at the outset instead of endeavouring to shirk their responsibility by turn- ing the sewage into the Brook in an untreated sate.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
GOOD TEMPLARY AT RUNCORN.

Th 'I Runcorn For ward Lodge 2444 held its weekly session on Ntonday last, being opened by the C T at 7 30. After the usual order of business had been disposed of, a new member was initiated. The pro- gramme for the evening, viz, "Question box night," was then carried out, when a most edifying time was spent, such questions as : Is the Temperance cause advancing ? Why is the Goad Templar Order the strongest Temperance Organization in the world ? What is the present avect of the Temper- ance cause? &c, being replied to by the various members, shewing that the various aspects of the Temperance question were well studied by those present. The borigelwas closed in the usual manner at 9 o'clock by Bro Anders, C T. CAST UP BY THE TIDE.

Toe body of -John Cawley, mate of the flat Char- lotte, belonging to the Rochdale Canal Company, was cast up by the tide at Hale in Me river Mersey on Saturday, and was taken to Weston Point. Cawley mysteriously disappeared from the flat ten days ago, when sailing between Liverpool and Runcorn. It is stated toat he went under ssveral aliaseQ, and that his real name was Robert Winter- bottom. His mother lives at Viratersheddings. He was about 30 years of age. The inquest was held on Tuesday at Weston a verdict of "Found drowned," being returned. SUICIDE OF AN OLD MAN AT HALTON.

1 On the sth instant the holy of an old tnn named Samuel Cookson aged 74, boatman, was found hanging by a rope from the roof of his bedroom. Information was given to the police and at the sub- sequent ioqueQt held by Nit. Dobson,county coroner, it transpired that the deceased had been out of work some time which bad preyed upon his mind. He had threatened to hang himself,but he wasibelieved to be only; joking,---A. verdict of, "Suicide while of unsound mini " was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN* NOTES
div.p: RUNCORN* NOTES
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

I learn on good authority that the Rev•J Osborne has resigned his office of Secretary to the Free Church Council. Thil step has, to a certain extent, been forced upon him by the action of a certain gentleman—a member of the Frae Church Council and a prominent local personage—who directly charged him with instigating the " re7o/utionary demonstration" held a fortnight ago. It is rumoured that certain passages of arms took place between the individuals concerned which, for the honour of Nonconformity, had better not see the light of print. The soberest individual would blush, and the more hot-headed would be indignant. Still it would only be just to the public to make all the facts known, Evict it is to be hoped, from Lt, pub- lic standpoint, that one of the gentlemen concerned will publish, sooner or later the entire circum- stances.

One thing certain is that Nfr Osborne's resigna- tion is a distinct lass to the Free Church Council in particular and local official Nonconformity in general. Thera are also pretty strong assurances from other promin6nt officials connected with tbe Council that there are likely to be other deflections if Mr Osborne refuses to reconsider his decision. Every right minded person will sympathise with Mr Osborne that he has been made the target of a most unfair attack.

The last of the festivities which should have been held in connection with the coronation have taken place, so Runcorn can now look forward once more to the trivial round and common task. Saturday was a great day and will never be forgotten, And had the elements been propitious the " Olde Englishe Sports" on the football field would also have gone down to local history with an untar- nished record. What the festivities would have been bad the Coronation taken place can be faintly imagined by what has already occurred. There is not the slightest doubt but the little Cheshire town would easily have held its own with any town of similar size. The next thing the "city fathers" will have to decide is whether the town is to have any further glorification when the coronation actually takes place. At present there is just a faint grumble from a certain class who think the festivi- ties:have been spread over a long enough period and who are in mortal dread lest further festivities bring further dislocation of trade. Perhaps a selfish view, as has be-,n asserted. But then self is the pre-dominant, partner in the majority of consti- tutions. Even Town Councillors and Parsons are not free from the taint.

div.head: KILLBD BY TAB KICK OF A HORSE.
div.p: KILLBD BY TAB KICK OF A HORSE.

_ Mr S Brighouse, County Coroner, held an inquest at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on Monday evening, into the circumstances attending the death of William Howells, a farm labourer, who was employed at the Hall House Farm, Ilaytiock, and who died at the farm on Sunday afternoon,after having been kicked by a mare the previous day, Mr John Latham was foreman of the jury, and Inspector Palmer watched the case in the interests of the police.—James Mason, of the Hall House Farm, said that about half-past tour on Saturday afternoon be saw the deceased take one of the horses into the stable at their farm. When leaving the stable deceased began to pat the horse on its hind quarters, but the animal kicked out, catching Howells in the abdomen, knocking him six feet away. Witness, with the help of a farm labourer took deceased into the house and he was put to bed Dr Gauge, of Earlestown, was called in the same night, but Howells died on Sunday.—ln answer to the Coroner, witness stated that they had had the horse on the farm six year. Deceased had been with them since May 17th. The animal was aged, and was a quiet horse. He had never known her to kick before.—The Coroner said it was a very ' simple case.—The jury returned a verdict of " dental death."

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY J ULY 11, 1902 INTERESIING ACTION IN THE RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. Alleged Assault by a Constable.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY J ULY 11, 1902 INTERESIING ACTION IN THE RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. Alleged Assault by a Constable.

At the Runcorn County Curt. on Tuesday, befo,e His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands. C.. a boy of 14 named Ern.st France, sued Constable Gregory for dam- ages for personal injuries committed on the 7th January, and claimed for the sum of £lO 10s.

The plaintiff's evidence showed that on the night in questioo France, with a boy named Albert Turn,r, was standing against Dobson's shop wnen P.C. Gregory walked along. The boy ran away followed by the police- man who ran him down Delph Bridge towards his own home. In Bold—Areet the constibte overtook him, and after hitting him twice with a cane collided with him and knocked him down. He afterwards hit him while on the ground. The boy shouted to the policeman " You have broken my knee." In a semi-conscious con- dition he was conveyed to Dr McDougaq's surgery, where he was attended by Dr Bethune, who ordered the ambulance and sent him horn'. Ele was confined to his bed for twelve week., the wound being at least four inches in length. The doctors bill amounted to £4 43 which with the additional ex- penses incurred am muted to £lO LO. The day after the accident occurred the defendant had called upon plaintiff's father awl said he would pay the doctor's hill. He had, however, since refused to pay when he foind it amounted to so much. The Case for the defence was that P.O Gregor:7 wee on duty in Bridge-street on the night in g144ti0.1 an that owing to complaints received he warm-d the defendant with other boys to desist from playing, on the parape:s. No sooner was his back turned than the boys Came back again. He then went to a shop and bought a, light 3 sue. He afterwards saw the defendaw with others and ran after him. The boy would not have been caught by Gregory but he fell down. France was never struck before he fell down but when Gregory caught him after be had fallen down he picked him up and struck him with the cane twice. It was denied that Gregory ever bromised the boy's father be would pay the doctor's bill. Wavas submitted that the constable was not responsible for the accident inasmuch as he had not knocked the boy down, and the further legal point was rats-d that as the bov had not instructed his father to engage a doctor, kc he could not legally recover.—Many witnesses were called on both sides and much cooflicting evi lance given. His Honour said that after carefulty reviewing the evidence he had elanilei till!: the plaintiff could not recover from the defendant. The boy had not been pushed down but had fallen down for which the con- stable was not iesponsioie.—Juogment for Abe defend- ant without costs. Mr Browne of Warrington repre- sented the plaict'ff and Mr 'crubshaw of Chester repre- sented the defendant--Colonel Harntnersley also watched the case.
A Former Newton Farmer and his Rent

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday' before His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K,C., an action was heard in which Lord Newton claimed £122 Os id, being arrears of rent due, from Thomas Mather formerly tenant of the Sand Hole Farm, Newton-le-Willows, but now residing in High-street —Mr A Browne, Warrington' (instructed by Mr Le=lie, ag-nt), re- presented Lord Newton, and Mr Milligan, of Wigan appeared on behalf of the defendant.—Mr Browne pointed out that judgment had been obtained for the amount due in the High Court and it was now remittal to that Court for an order of payment. The defendant had acted so shabbily and disgracefully in the matter that Lord Newton was determined to make the defendant pay the amount due. When the defendant left the farm he received £5O from Mr Boydell, the incoming tenant, on condition that it was paid to Lord Newton's agent toward) the rent due. Instead of paying the money to his landlo-d, the defendant gave the money to his wife who was conducting a small business at Newton.—ln cross-examination by Mr Browne, the defendant sta,ed that the sale of his stock and furniture realised a little over £4OO. He paid out of it £233 to Lord Newton's agent for one year's rent, and of the balance some went to pay creditora and the rest he pave to his wife. She advanced him money to go on the farm. He never promised Mr Hayden, the incoming tenant, that he would pay the £5O to Lord Newton'e agent. It was true that his wife bought in most of the furniture at the sale.—Mr Milligan said the defendant was in a very unfortunate position. He farmed the place in question for eight years and his wife lent him from time to time from £3OO to £4OO. He continued losing money on the place and he determined to sell what stock he had. From the sale he realised £450. Out of this sum he paid a year'e rent £233 and with the remainder he paid the expenses of the sale and his creditors. His wife took the remain- der towards the money she had lent. She was now carrying on a small business at a toffy shop in High-street.—Mr Browse stated that unless the defendant had given an undertaking to band over the money received from the in- coming tenant he would not have permitted Mr Boydell to come in at the time he did.—Mr Milligan said the defendant was 63 years of age and unable to work.—Mr Browne said proceedings would not have been taken if the defendant had acted in a reasonable manner.—His Honour made an order for the amount claimed, to he paid at the rate of £1 a month.

The prepar-ations in connection with the b tnar being promoted for the purpose tof raiQing funds towards the erection of a Cottage Hospital, are almost completed, and given fine weather it should be attended with success. Every effort has been put forward to make it attractive, and there will be no dearth of amuoements. The object is a laudable one, and, notwithstanding the cold water whilh a certain few have endeavoured to throw over ir, it cannot be denied that the provi4ion of a hospital,on no matter how small a scale, if it tends to the alleviation of suffering cannot but redound to the credit of those who have sacrified time and labour to that end. The bar= will extend over three days,commencing on Thursday next,and it is hoped that the financial result will be beyond anticipa- tion.

It appears that the District Council have decided to again increase the price of gas to consumers to the extent of twopence per thougand feet. This will mean two advances in twelve months, without any corresponding increase in quali...y. It is said that there has been a loss in production, and that if there is a surplus consequent upon the increase in price, there may be a revision in the charges. The Council are endeavouring to popularise the use of gas stoves by householders,with the view of increas- ing the consumption of gas, but they hold out very I little encouragement to people to purchase gas stoves, when they increase Vie price of gas and practically put a veto upon the innovation so far as working people are concerned. In other towns I the stoves are supplied free of charge, and fixed in the houses at the &tine price, but here the people have not only to pay for the stove, but have to pay an increased price for the privilege of using the Council's gas. What is doae in other towns cal be done here, and a quality of gas for cooking could be supplied at a cheaper rata. At any rate the matter is well worth the cansiderCion of the Coun- cil if they want the stove idea to be a success.

A notice has been served by the Provincial Elec- tric Supply and Traction Company, to the effect that they intend to apply to the Board of Trade for authority to supply electricity for public purposes in the Newton-in-51akerfield district, This, it is presumed will be the outcome of the Light Rail- ways, which will be running through the di•trict shortly, and doubtless the innovation will be very welcome. It is to be hoped the supply will be available to householders, and that it will be oh' ain- able at a cheaper rate than the gas. In any case we should have a better, cleaner and more brilliant illuminant

div.head: TO SCARBOROUGH. A Flying Visit with Warrington Trippers.
div.p: TO SCARBOROUGH. A Flying Visit with Warrington Trippers.
[By Quilp 'N I

j In his desire to obtain a complete change from every-day surroundings the Warrington day tripper is often led to visit distant resorts, but it is very seldom in teed that be ventures so far afield as Scarborough. This is not to be wondered at, when it is considered that a trip to the charming Yorkshire watering place entails a railway journey varying in duration from four to five hours or more lOn Saturday last, however, about twelve hundred inhabitants of " the good old town," accomplished this along journey, and had ten hours at their disposal in which to sea the sights "of Scar- borough. The directors of Messrs. Pater Walker and Son, Limited, acted wisely and considerately in selecting Scarborough as the venue of this year's excursion in connection with the firm, for many , people of the working class who would otherwise, for obvious reasons, never think of visiting the East Coast, were thus afforded an opportunity of ' appreciating the charms of a resort whicn ranks high in point of natural beauty. Having been deputed to accompany the excur- sion, I found myself in Horsemarke.-street at an hour when lam usually wrapt in slumber-4 45 a. in. Strains of music broke the quietude which gener- ally hovers over the main streets at this time, and on reaching the station I found the Brewery Band, resplendent in uniforms of green and gold,discours• log lively selections. It was a good-humoured crowd which thronged the plattorm above. " Will the weather be fine ?" was the questioo uppermost in their minds. "It always is fine for Walker's trip " was the remark of many who maintained a cheery optimism. Other, having regard to the previous night's unpromising conditions, and to the threatening sky overhead:were less sanguine. The first train had already steamed in,and was'ere this nearly filled. The brewery officials were hurrying hither , and thither, unremitting in their efforts to ensure that the long.anticipated outing snould not be marred by any hitch which it was in their power to prevent. I had just taken nay seat in the saloon provided for the office staff, when the whistle sounied shrilly, and the train with its human freight was 800 n speeding on its way,to be followed ten minutes later by a second train. At some places through which we passed, cotton operatives could be seen wen ling their was to the mills, and one could not help contrasting their prospect for the morning with that of the merry trippers. Some delightfully picturesque hill scenery mat the , eyes of the passengers between Stockport and Penistone. Tee sun was now shining radiantly,and, bathed in his glorious rays, the country around I looked charming. After sun try stoppages the ancient city of York was reached at half-past eight; and there was much waving of handkerchiefs when the excursionista perceived the second train steam- ing along behind. After passing through the ' station, a good view of the grey old Minster was to ihe obtained. After leaving York the journey became decidedly wearisome, and all were glad when the train draw up at Scarborough. On the programme of the arrangements for the excursion it was stated that the 1 railway c)cnpanies " proposed to make the j )urnoy to Scarborough under four hours." The time actually occupied was five hours and ten minutes ! Warrington was left promptly ht five, and it wss ten minutes pist ten when the trippers arrived at their journey's end. The second train, nf course, foil iwed a little later. Ho ! refreshing it Was, after being so long in a railway carriag, to feel tee invigorating effects of a cool sea breeze! _

It is; about twenty years. saece Messier Walker hit upon the happy idea of giving their employees an annual out- log, and I sin told that every excursion has been favoured with fine weather. Saturday's trip waa, for- tunately, its exception to the rule, the conditions belay,' ideal. Throueheut the day the sun shone brilliantly from an azure sky,whilst a breeze from the sea tempered ' the heat. A-id now to a brief survey of Siarboreuge. After journeying such a great distance, it was only natural that the excursionists should expect to field something out of the ordinary to repay them. I think it may truthfully be said that they were not disappointed. " Searberough the beautiful "—as it is aptly called— has been singularly well blesaed by nee ure Such ii its climate that trees and flowers flouLish almost at the water's edge, and this in its.lf constitute; an advantage which is lacking at many resorts. To obtain a compre- hensive view of Scarborough one should asceol the Castle Hill—a rugeed eminence which: divides the town into two distinct portions, and which is crowned by the remams of what was once a streng fortress. Accom- panied by a friend I turned my step; thither, an i the delightful proep,et which met our gezi wag ample compensation for the stiff climb. Scarborough can boast of two magnificent bays—the senth bay and the north bay. First let U 3 direct our attention to the south side. The placid blue waters of the bay are dotted with innumerable small craft, filled with happy pleasure seekers. Looking immediatelyfbelow we seethe ancient part of the town, with its harbour and lighthouse and quaint red-roofed houses. A little to the right stands the grand old Parish Church which dates its foundation from the twelfth century. Cast the eye further to the south, and we see " new Sear- borough." Here are tha Spa buildings and grounds, the prettily laid out Holbeek gardens, and the f ashion- able splanade. Still fur.her on, the bold headlands , which enclose the bee, jut out in striking contrast. , Inland is the richly wooded Olivea'r Mount—to called from a legend that Crirnw,ll planted his gins on it, to ' ere upon the town. And new to the north side. Terre is net nearly so much life and activity here, Probably many of the day trippers would leave Scarborough un- aware that there is a north bay. The view in this direction is just as charming as on the Routh side. There are some beautiful gardens (called the Clarence Gardens, as they were opened by the late Duke of Clar- ence)—in fact the public gezelens constitute one of Scarborough's most charming features, A fine drive— the Royal Albert drive—runs at the foot of the Clarence Gardens and the work is now in progress of continuing Ithis drive round the base of the Castle Hill, se as to con- nect the north and gouth sides of the town. Dmcmding the Castle Hill, I paused at the Church yard to see the tomb of Anne Brontii, sister of the famous novelist. With much interest I also inspected the Parish Church, in which there is much aristic decorated work. A visit to Scarborough—if only for • day—would not be com- plete without a visit to the Valley Park, which lies in , the centre of the town. It is splendidly wooded, and an hour may be pleasantly whiled away beneath the shade of the tall spreading trees. To all appearances, the Warrington trippers enj iyed themselves inamensele. The manifold attractions on the sands,of course,came in for a great deal of attention and large groups of exenraiouists could be seen watching the arrice of the marionettes, the feats of the " strong man," and the ever popular entertainments of the pierrots. Many took advantage of the opportunity of having a sea trip, whilst others, who preferred to remain on terra firma had drives in the town and surrounding country. Train time at length came, and at nine o'clock all the excursionists were on their way home. The journey was a tedious!one, and many of the passengers,tiredfout with the exertio is of the day,seught well earned repose. There were others, however, not so inclined, and they endeavoured to enliven the monotony with song. The band, too,gave several selections,and it was appropriate that at one station they should play " Lead 'kindly light." It was ten minutes past two when Warrington was reached, and the excursion of 1902 was an event of the past.

Cairo-street Sunday School Holiday. On Saturday, June 28th, 67 children and adults connected with the above school started on their second annual holiday to Gime Hucklow via Millers Dale. Starting from Central Station at 3.15, they journeyed to Miller's Dale, where waggonettes were waiting to convey the party and their luggage to the holiday home, Great Hucklow. The house is beautifully situated on the side of the hill over- looking the village.—The party en:ioyed themselves very much during the week, the weather on the whole being fine.—On Monday nay were conveyed in waggonettes to Haddon Hall, which was inspec- ted with great interest and pleasure, after whi.do lunch was partaken OF, and the party started on , their return journey, stopping at Chatsworth House just long enough to go through the house and grounds, getting back again about 7 o'clock On Tuesday the weather being rather dull, the time was spent around the home. On Wednesday morn- ' ng the adults visited Eyam churchyarl, where a iablet is erected'in honour of the brave men who lost t eir lives turough the great plague which broke ut in this village. They afterwards visited the natural pulpit in the delf where the Rev Monpessor used to preach to the villagers during this trying period. Thursday morning being fine about 50 of tha party decided to walk to Castleton a distance of about six miles A visit wai paid to the Speed- well mine, this mine having been sunk 120 years ago at the cast of .£14,000. The miners cut their way through solid rook for 750 yards, working at this for eleven years night and day. On Friday most of the adults visit-cl Buxton, this town being about twelve miles distant,, and a most enjoyable day was spent. Saturdaybeing the last day of the visit the party wera very busy getting ready for the return journey, leaving the Home about 10 15 to catch the 11.43 train from Millers Dale station, they arrived at Warrington at 1.20, everybody hav- ing spent a most jolly week.
•THE COrIONATION•

div.head: Warrington Friendly Societies Postponed Procession.
div.p: Warrington Friendly Societies Post- poned Procession.

The Warrington Friendly Societies' Committee in charge of the procession for the Coronation, at their meeting on Monday night, decided not to be disbanded, but to adjourn sine die, to be called together again when an official date is given for theCoronstion to take place. The societies will take part in the celebration upon the day selected by the Mayor. and Corporation. It was further decided to have a picnic to .tester on Saturday, August 9th.

div.head: CORONATION CELEBRATIONS AT RUNCORN. A Monster Procession
div.p: CORONATION CELEBRATIONS AT RUNCORN. A Monster Procession

It was a great day at Burnam nn Saturday. Neyer in the history of tbe towa has there ever been previ- ously seen rued • procession. Far once all the Sunday Schools were combined in one parade and the spectacle presented was one never to be forgotten. Tbe day was brilliantly fine and everything conspired to make the occasion a memorable one, Al toe shopkeepers closed their establishments from twelve noon to six in the evening, and as the workmen also had their half holiday the streets presented a crowded appearance. The starting point was fixed for three o'clock from the Market Hall, but prior to that time all the Sunday Schools had massed in their alloted positions and pre- sented a magnificent spectacular display. Each school was headed 03 its banner and throughout, the thin line of scholars and adherents who were enrolled under the folds of the flag were numerous banners, bannerettes and floral devices. Toe majority oh the ,schools,too,had within their ranks numbers of ladies and gentlemen, and hors and girls, representing different characters: There were several kings and queens in Coronation robes attended be their suite ; there were ambassadors from every country 'neath the sun ; many were historical, some mythological, stid more patriotic. Many designs were intricate and displayed cunningness of thought and subtlety of execution. o.bers were simple in the extreme, but none the less pretty and effective. There were representations of Morris dancers, khaki boys, dairy maids, haymakers, sailors and fishers, flag drill boys, jockeys, 80-peep, Boy Bale, Turks, " buttons," pages, Diggers, policemen, Pierrota, clowns, Arabs, Calnamen, "to hats." Englisnmen (red, white, and blue), archers, cricketers, soldiers, bakers, millers, footballers, &c Everything showed that time, money and skill had been mast lavishly expended by those interested to render the pageant as strikingly suecessful as passible. What the procession would have been had it taken place on the day arranged when public interest was at its heieht, is imeessible to imagine. It is, how- ever, easy to estimate the striking spectacle produced I by the grouping together of such a vast concourse of brilliantly attired persons. The throng was enormous and from the platform erected by the Rouutain nought could be seen save a sea of heads issuing from the Market-place down the leading thoroughfare, It three o'clock • prompt the Weston Wesleyan Band took their stand on the raised dais, draped with royal red, aid conducted'by Mr W Handley, played the opening staves of "God Save the King." After the mometary hush the national by ant rya-, tarn. LI) with the utmost hearti- ness by the entire multitude and sung to the finish. The seemingly chaotic mass then resolved itself into an orderly procession with the utmost regularity and with- out the slightest hitch—a circumstance which speaks remarkably well for the marshalle,Measrs G IT Kirkham, W E Dudley and J Scragg. Inspector Egerton, who ' had er,tire charge :of tee palice:arrangements, led the way supported by Sergeant Cooper and Constables Bowyer, and Nicholls. After these gentlemen in blue came the Weston Wesleyan band (conductor, Mr John Smith), behind which walked the Chairman of the Urban District Council, Mr Samuel Taylor (wearing the Jubilee chain of office), members of the magistracy, councillora,rand others. The magistrates present were Messrs F J Norman, A R Norman, R H Poenett, E Imison, and J Pritchard, with the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr Johnson), whilst amoagst other gentlemen holding public offices whol followed here and elsewhere in the procession were Councillors M J Sweetmarn T Jones,l3 J Griee, G H Kirkham, W Handley, G Hewitt, 8 Walton, J Wileou, and D Bisbrown, the Rev J Chalmers, Mr W J Cunningham, Mr J M Fcitti, Mr W Hankinsen, Mr J Littler, Mr R ttawlinson' Mr 1 Riley, Mr J Sayln, Mr J Turnbull, Mr J )hu F Moulton, Mr Edwin Marshall (secretary to the Urban Council), Mr Walter Jones (assistant secretary), Mr Michael Barker (consulting surveyor), Mr James Wilding (surveyor and water euchre:l), Mr T A Lawrenson kneadmaster of the !natl. tnte Day Schools), Mr James Percival (sanitary an- ent-niter), Mr Thomas Baote (exarninsr of canal boats), and others. " Old Brunswick " leading the van, fol- lowed them p ublic officials leading the United N mcinformist and Catholic scheels, the Anglican body , choesin; to walk in a united body at the rear of the other scheola. The Hope Hall contingent were led by their band, the Salvation Army band was also in evidence, and the St Edward's Roman Catholics likewise had a; band of their own. In the united procession of Church of England schools toe way was led by tlae buglers of the Runcorn Volunteers, a sailors' fife band was with tho Mersey Mission, tile Salt Works bend treaded the Holy Trinity Church Sunday Scheel, and the Runcorn Volunteer Band (conductor, Mr W Outhaaite) iaspirited the marching of the Parish Church contingent The Vicar,and his curates brought up the rear of a proceosion which was nearly two milts in length, The route followed was that selected in the first instanced namely :—From, the Markel-place via Church-street. terloo-road, Waterloo-bridge, Lowlands-road, Snaw- street, Green way-road, High-street, Bridge-street, Halt-re-road, to the Crane, where the procession turned and later on they filed off to the resnectiTo stboolE at Delph Briege. The entire route was lined with crowds of people and every window seemed to be crowded with spectators. At the respective schools tea was provided for the scholars, which gave an additional zest to the proceedings. It is stated that the numbers of the several bodies were as follows :—Brunswick Wes- leyan Methodist, 564 ; Camden Wesleyan Methodist,4oo; Hope Hall Mission, 120 ; Ashbridge-street Mission, 90 ; Salvation Army, 80 ; Haiton-road Wesleyan Methedist, 360 ; Primitive Methodist, Cireenway-road, 244 ; St Edward's Roman Catholic, 280 ; St John's Presbyterian, 200 ; Bethesda Coneregation.l, 210 ; Nelson-street Wes- leyan Methodist, 130 ; St Luke's Congregational. 184 ; Elesmere-street United Methodist, 152 ; Mersey Mission to 8-amen, 300; St Michael's Cburch,36o ; Holy *l'rinity Mill Brow Mission (Ragged School), 260 ; Hely Trinity Church, 400; Parish Church. 924 ; total, 5,258. 1 There can be no question but the pageant was an Im- posing and a brilliant one and reflected the highest credit on all connected with it. Youth and Age, Poverty and Luxury, contributed their quota and the spectacle must ever live memorable in toe annals of local histcry.

div.head: Old English Sports.
div.p: Old English Sports.

Tile old English sports which should have been held in connection with the Coronati7n festivities were held os Wednesday evening on the Runcorn Football field. Despite the very inclement weather there was a very large avendance and considerable interest was mani- fested in the proceedings probably owing to it being the first time in local history that anything similar has been held in the tiwn or district. The maj irity of the public men were present on the grand stand Mr S Taylor and Mr F Norman being conspicuous in counteninceing the sports. Most of the races were very keenly contested the winner generally coming in tor a well merited ovation.

Be soon recovered coasciousncss, and no ill results are feared. ..--.4.---. Baptist Church, Warrington.
Re-opening Services and Settlement.of Pastor.

Notwithstanding the internee heat large congregations assembled at the above place of worship on Sunday last. The day had been looked forward to with great antici- pation as it 10113 a time of double importance in the history of the church. For about 12 mouths the church has been without a pastor and during that time the pulpit has beea filled by supplies. Some nine months ago Mr Dunnico (while on his vacation) came and occu- pied the pulpit for a Sunday, with the result that at the close of the day'a services the general opinion was that lit possible the church should secure him as its pastor. Time went on and the feeling amongst the church and congregation grew stronger and became so manifest that the church eventually gays him a unanimous call to the pastorate. After due consideration of the matter , and notwithstanding that he had bad several calls from lother churches and some much larger than Golborne- street, he decided to accept the call and become its pastor. The church had begun to look dirty and in need of several repairs, and as soon as the date of the Rev Herbert Dunnico's settlement was definitely known, it was decided to have it put into a• fit condition for his ministry. For the last month the place has been closed and has undergone a state of repair and decora- tion. -aloe exterior has been attended to but more especially the interior. Here several imerovoments have bees carried out, new lights have been pue in, the organ rebuilt, and the rostrum fumigated, stained and var- nished, with the result that on Sunday last the place presented a happy and pleasing appearance. The cost of the whole renovation was £lOO, and it was endeavoured by the services on Sunday last to raise this amount and so be cleared from debt. Efforts had been made to make the service as bright and er joyable as possitle, especially the musical part. The choir in the evening gave the anthem " Send out Thy light" arid at the afternoon service Miss Ethel Ratebone gave a solo and in the evening sang " The better land." Mr Dunnica erne, has studied at the Miellaed University College and Rawdon College, Yorks, preached special sermons and gave an address in the afternenn. The morning sermon was based upon the worth Luke 10. v. 33, and after a brief reference to the parable and the carefulness of the Good Samaritan the preacher said that the Chririan life was divided into stages and the first stage of the Christian service was that which com- menced with a provision. Whatsoever our charge was at the beginning it seemed easy and we never thought that some day our provision would be exhau tad and we I should have to look up for more. When the morning was fresh with dew and the wind of life sang freshly in our ears we never dreamt that the day would come when we should be tired and weary and unwell. We were told to count the cost but that is impossible for the Christian until he s' wide on the other si ie. To charge oneself with one soul involved at times terrible sacrifice, hut to charge oneself with hundreds—who could tell what that meant P A minister's work was in some senses the most depressing of all work. The final stage of Christianity which the preacher spoke upon at some length was when we discovered that the secret of all lasting sorvies was love to Christ. From the earliest ' days of the Christian church down to the present, those ' who had done most service for man had done it because they loved the Master. B.cause we love Him we keep His commandments, we love Him first and that love is the secret of serviee. At the afterneara aervice,the pastor gave an address in which be said he WI! glad to be there in order that he might identify himself mitts the Sunday School. Toe Sunday echoel had been one of the most important factors in his life and they might rest assured that he wauld he no stranger in their mi Ist. There could be no nobler work and they would ever find in him a true faced and rine who would ever be at their service. At the evening service the church was crowded the discourse being taken from Hebrews 11 v. 35.36. After referring to tee gloiy roll the preacher went on to speak about the wisdom of the writers appeal. Great men were the measure of a great race and revealed the p;teat'al.ty of the race. 7 hey were a mark to press forward to, an ideal o aim a', a standard to measure be. In c.inclesioe t',ei preacher said that the selidicy of a church was quite as real as that of a race and if they were to be suceeesful in their work together, then each memb,r high or low must be pre- pared to do his share aed till his nicee. Collections were taken 2t each service.ani the total cluo3.loes, elections See., amaunted to £B6.

div.head: NARRINGTON CYCLISTS Al BEESTON.
div.p: NARRINGTON CYCLISTS Al BEESTON.
"President's Day."

Saturday was " President's Day " in connection with the Warrington Cycling Club, and once more the mem- bers were entertained at Beesten Tower, the charmingly situated reeidence of the president, Mr John Naylor. Ideal weather favoured the event, and there was a strong muster of members, including many ladies. The majority made the journey by read, and had a pleasant ride through Acton Bridge and Ouddington. The ladies and a few gentlemen travelled by the 2.15 train to Chester. Here, a stop of over an hour was neceseary, and the party took advantage of the delay to visit the river and parks, which are new looking just at their best. Resuming the journey, Beeston was reached at about five o'clock, the cyclists baying already arrived. Unfortunately they had bad a mishap on the road, Mr Walter Booth colliding with a cart and spraining his wrist, which necessitated his return home. At the Tower,the visitors were met by Mr Naylor who cordially welcomed each one. The addition ts the house, which was commenced about two years ago,is now practically completed, and its excellent appearance wee the chief topic of conversation. In design it is an exact copy of Mereton Old Hall, and the eequisite carving in various parts was freely admired. The woodwork of the building is all of solid English oak. The whole of the house and extension was thrown open for inspection—a privilege which was greatly appreciated. From the top of the tower a delightful view of Beeston, Peckforton and the district around was obtained. An adjourn- ment was made to the shady tennis court at the side of the house, where Mr Naylor provided an excellent tea. Mr and Mrs Naylor and their guest, the vicar of Bees- ton, sat down with the party. The meal over, an im- promptu coneert was held on the lawn. Songs were very cr nlitebly rendered by Messrs J Davenport, F A Field- house, and J Einson. TRO humorous serge of Mr Eason were especially well received. Mr J Finch made a very effieent accompanist, and he alao played music for dancing. During the interval The VICAR ow BEESTON took the opportunity of saying how much he was indebted to Mr and Mns Naylor for their kind invitation, Although he was unknown th most of them be thought it was a great treat to be amongst a lot of men. He had had a great deal te do with men in his time, and he always managed to get on with them. They ought to feel themselves very lucky in having such friends as Mr and Mrs Naylor, and they appreciated their kindness in no small measure. In living in a p'ace like Beemten tbev were very fortunate to have people like Mr and Mrs Naylor. (Hear. bear.) He hoped that would not be the last time he would have the privilege of meeting the Warriceten cyclists. He asked for three cheers for Mr and Mrs Naylor and wished them long life and prosperity, and hoped they would have many more of those happy Saturday afternoons (Applause). Three hearty cheers were given and " For he's a jolly good fellow " heartily sung. Me" Pa " Davies said he would like to support the remarks of their worthy Vicar. He (the Vicar), had taken the wind "out of him "—(laughter)—and ex- pressed exactly the sentiments he was about to utter on behalf of himself and the Warrington Cycling Club.Tbev (the club) knew Mr Naylor's good work, and Warring- ton knew it too. They highly appreciated his kindness to them, on that occasion particularly. The last time they met, the country was plunged in'the throes of war. I Now, there was peace, and as the last bulletin on the King's health was favourable they had geod cause to re- joice. He would net like that opportunity to pass without expressing, on behalf of the Warrington Cycling Club, their gratitude to Mr Naylor. (Applause.) Mr NAYLOR, in reply, said he was much obliged to them for their kind remarks. The weather, as usual, was " Naylor's Weather," and be was very pleased to see that the Warrington Club had come up to their past reputation and brought a lot of nice ladies with their. He was glad to see them, and hoped they weuld all come another year. They were favoured not only by the glorious weather but by the preseace or the ladies. (Hear, bear.) _ . _ . . . . . .

, At about eight o'clock the party left for Warrington. Those travelling by traii retailed horns shortly after nine, and the cyclists who bad a glorious ride through Delansere Fcrest, arrived at headquarters about eleven.

Dearth of Magistrates. On Saturday morning the business at the War- rington Police Court was delayed for over half an hour, only one magistrate (Mr J W Hayward) having put in an appearance. Communication by telephone failed to produce any result, the gentle- men appealed to being either not at home or unable to come. Three cases were on the list, and as each required the jurisdiction of two magistrates, they could not be proceeded with. However, after nearly ball an hour had passed, a messenger procured the services of Mr Thornton. The cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
The Affairs of Bishop and Company Limited.

At the sitting of the Chancery Court, at St. George's Hall, Liverpool. on Monday, before Sir Samuel Hall, K.C. (vice-chancellor), the deben- ture holders' action' brought by Messrs. Redley and Waterhouse against W A Bishop and Co, Limited, who carry on business in Warriagtora as manufaT- turers of borax, was mentioned by Mr Rutherford, who said that an application was made to his honour last week, and a receiver and manager ap- pointed. Notice of motion was served upon the de- fendants on Friday, but they did not appear, and under the circumstances he thought the best course was to continue the receiver and serve a fresh notice of motion.—The Vice-Chancellor said if the defendants appeared beforethe Registrar and con- sented the order could be made, but in the mean- time the matter would stand over till:next Monday the receiver being con,,inued. and also Ca e under- taking given by the defendants.

div.head: Interesting Wedding at St. Paul's Church.—.
div.p: Interesting Wedding at St. Paul's Church.—.
Spinks—Massey:

The marriage was solemnized at St Paul's Church on Tuesday morning of Dr Henry Spinks, of Wigan (son of the late Dr C N spike, of Warrington), to Miss Elizabeth (Lizzie) Massey, (third daughter of Mr and Mrs Frederick Massey, of 16, Bewsey-place, Bewsey-road). The officiating clergyman was the Vicar of the parish, the Rev William Bracecamp. The bride who was given away by her father, wore a grey silk voile dress trimmed with old lace, a grass lawn toque trimmed with French roses and pink satin, and a gold brooch with diamonds and rubies, the gift of the bridegroom. She carried a shower bouquet of white roses and lilies of tbe valley, also the gift of the bridegroom. The brides- maids, Mies Nellie Massey (sister of the bride) and Miss Ethel Spinks (sister of the bridegroom), wore dresses of pink silk voile, trimmed with old lace and black picture hats. They carried shower bouquets, and wore gold brooches, also the gift of the bridegroom. Mr Chris Spinks (brother of the bridegroom) acted as best man. Mr R Evans, AR CO, (in the absence of Mr Ernest Wilkes, the organist of the church) presided at the organ, and contributed an excellent selection, of music from such composers as Liszt, Widor, Rigor. and Mendelssehn, the favourite wedding march of the last named being played as the happy couple left the church after signing the register. The hymn sung, in which the congregation heartily joined, was "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden." Mr and Mrs Spinks, as well as the guests were subjected to the usual shower of rice and confetti as they returned to the carriages in waiting for them. The wedding breakfast took place at No 16, BewseY- road, the residence of the bride's parents, a large number of guests being present. In the afternoon the happy couple left for London, en route for the South Coast, the bride's travelling dress being of navy blue, trimmed with black glace. She wore a Tuscan hat. A large number of handsome presents were received,

div.p: A FATAL DIVE.
Sad Death of a Clerk at Winwick Waterworks.

At the " General Elliott" Hotel, Croft, on Monday afternoon, Mr SI Brighouse, county coroner, resumed an inquest relating to the death of Alexander Graham, 28, timekeeper and clerk, of Lady-lane, Croft, who died on the 26th June, from the effects of diving down one of the new wells, containing 120 ft. of water,which is being sunk at Middleton, Winwick, for the Warrington Cor- poration. Neil M Barron, resident engineer for the Warrington Corporation, st teed that Messrs George Lawson,cf Blair- both and Ruthergeo, near Glasgow, were contractors for the work, and decmsed was employed by them as time- keeper and clerk. For some weeks deceased had been engaged in diving operations, Messrs Lawson had de- cided to engage a professional diver to remove scaffolding left at the bottom of the well, but Graham wanted to do the work himself, and asked witness to give a certificate to the effect that he had done it. in order that be might become a professional diver. Messrs Lawson had sent a diving suit from Scotland. De:teamed related to witness having had previous diving experi- ence at Wicklow, in Ireland. On June 4 Graham went down the well once, on June 7 twice, and once on the 9th, 10th, 11th, and 13th ult., on the latter date re- ceiving injuries to one of his acres which incapacitated him until the 6:h ult., when he descended once. On the following day, however, he went down the NO. 2 well five times, first at 10.30 a.m., when he stayed down 15 minutes, next at 11.10 a.m. for 20 minutes, at 2.40 o.m. for 35 minute., at 3.40 for 45 minutes, and at 5.10 for 35 minutes. len minute after reaching the surface on the last necasiso Graham was seiz.ld with illness, and was carried to the office where, despite his entreaties to the contrary, he was at eight o'clock attended by Dr Bennett, of Warrinyton. He died next morning at eight o'clock at home. Witness explained that deceased was very strong headed, and was one who wanted to get on in life.

In answer to the Coroner,witness:said he thought it was the excessive work of :going down five times in one day for such a long period that had caused Graham's death Witness had cautioned him about staying down so long, and also against coming to the surface too quickly. Ho would deicend in four or five minutes,instead of taking half an hour. Witness held the life line for deceased, and on signalling to him to come up, which he did three times, deceased signalled back that he was all right. There was greater risk in forcibly hauling a diver up than in allowing him to stay down, as the life line might have got entangled in the ladder which went down to the bottom. The well was only 12 feet 8 inches in diameter.

In reply to Major Roe (his Majesty's inspector -of factories and workshops), witness said Graham was net medically examined beim.° undertaking the work ; the rules, which accompanied the diving suit, stated that it should be dime when possible. But deceased had spoken about his previous experience in Wicklow, and witness considered him physically fit ta go down the well. The water pressure at the bottom would be 521 b. to the square inch There was no dial to the air-pump te show that too much air was being forced down, and, though it might be a desirable thing, contractors generally did not attach indicators to such air-pumps. He dig not consider the absence of an indicator a defect in the plant. By the Coroner : Witness did not take any responsi- bility for the contractor's apparatus, and the reason he held the life line was at deceased's particular request, as he (Graham) did not know anyone else there whom he regarded as perfectly safe to hold it. Witness held it simply as a favour to deceased. By Major Roe : Witness was in charge of the works, and could have ordered deceased not to go down, but did not consider the operation dangerous. Although witness had no responsibility in regard to the apparatus, he was in charge of the works. After hearing further evidence, _
The jury returned a verdict ef " Miiad veatcre," and exonerated everyone from blame.

rho Coroner remarked upon the very great assistance Mr Barron had Wen to them, and hoped he would not consider the examination by himself and Major Roe as being in any way detrimental to him. If ha did, he must take it from him (the coroner) that it was n,,t so. He had done everything he could under the circum- stances. '
