div.head: LECTURE ON "THE PILGRIM'S PROGRESS."
div.p: LECTURE ON "THE PILGRIM'S PROGRESS."

On Monday evening the Rev E Lloyd Jones dclivered an interestieg lecture on "The Pilgrim'e Progress." Mr James Dodds presided and was supported en the rostrum by the It, vo C H Hcckeu, T Bishop, and E Lloyd-Jones, and Mr T Birchen. There wee a fair attendance. In the course of his remarks, the Chairman said he had watched Silver-street scholars in their dark and early days. He had also reen their advance and success, as the result of the efforts of Mr Guest and his coadjutors, ant had rejaiced to see the schools take the position which they had taken among the day schools of Warrington. Be did net intend to speak upon the present positron of the education question- He made that remark in erder to put his friends Mr Hocken and Mr Bishop quite at ease. (Laughter.) Continuing. Mr Dodds said the subject of the lecture ought to be of the utmost interest to every Christian. It had boon said that there was nothing happeer than to turn from the books of the hcur to the books of all times, and he was quite sure that , they could not do better that eight than spend a little time upon a book which was at any rate the second best bock in the wce Id. In conclusion,the speaker expressed regret that the attendance was not larger. The Rev E LLOYD JONES Said he was not disappointed at the attendance, knowing that it was at Warrington. (Laughter.) Be would have been disappointed anywhere else, but he came there out of lo,s love and respect to hi 3 good friend Mr Guest, and if there had been only two or three present, he would have said every word that he had got to say. It was over twe hundred rears since John Bunyan finished his earthly pilgrimage to enter into the Eternal City. He was barn in the year 1628 and died in 1688, and was fifty years of age when he wrote "The Pilgrim's Progress." He (the speaker) always thought that the sixty years of Bunyan'e life were the most remarkable sixty in the history of this country—remarkable in that it pleased God then to give a larger number ef great men than he had ever given either before or after in sixty years. The charac- teristic feature of the present day was the absence of great men. He did not know in any department of life of a superbly great man. Not in literature, art, pulpit, sr press, did he know of a single character that ought not to be complimented if be (the speaker) said he was a good second class. Ho did not think, however, that the fact that there were so many great men living in his time, was the eliehteet advan`aee to Bunyan, He could not identify a single thought that Banyan berre wed from any of his great contemporaries,. If ever there was an original man,that man was John Bunyan, and if ever there was an original book, that book was "The Pil- grina's Progrese" The lecturer proceeded to give some reasons for the popularity of the book. The first was that a reader of the book formed the impression that the author was " thinking at first hand." He never described something that anyone else had seen or heard; everything he said and everything he wrote he had seen and felt first head. He (the sneaker) did not know how much It took to shock the people in Warrington, hut he would say this in trepidation;that "Pilgrim's Proems " was the first novel ever written In the English language, and thous- ands of dear Christian people who bed lived and died condemning novels had read "Pilgrim's Progress" many times over and thanked GO for it, net knowing that it was a novel. (Laughter.) Mr Jones dealt with seine of the 200 characters in the" Pilgrim's Progress." The names, he said, were se suggestive and expository that sometimes they did not want to know anything more about a pilgrim than the name. Goo* they had the name they had the character. If anyone asked him what was the most essential book for a preacher to master and which would be most helpful to him ha would say at once "Pilgrim's Progress," because there was no other book so far as he was aware that would as help a preacher or teacher to understand human nature, and he contended that te understand human nature was essential to all teaching. The undenominational- lain ef the book had helped it a great deal, No one could tell by reading it te what Church Bunyan belonged. Supremely it was a book dealing with the infirmities and the weaknesset et temple; and for that reason it was more Christian, for the essence of the Gospel was net denunciation of si•, but sympathy with the weak Notwithstanding the charm of the book it had had many adverse criticisms. They were told that Bunyan made the Christian life toe doleful. Many eritics laid " Pilgrim's Progress " could not be a religi- ous bock for the young people especially of the:2oth century. They did not like pilgrimage. They pre- ferred an excursion. The great craving of the age was that relieinn might be ease. There was one thing that ceuld not be mate easy. That was the art af being good Then they were told that Bunyan made too free use of the elements of fear, but the book appealed to every other faculty as well as rear. The last great objec- tion came from their friends the clergy. The clerical mind bated " Pilgrim's Progress " liko the devil. There were thousands of godly ministers in the 'Church of England who loved it as much as he did, hut they were not clerics. The clerical mind hated "Pilgrim's Progress " because from the City of Des- truction ter the Heavenly Kingdom there was nos a parson knocking about anywhere. (Laughter.) There were ministers in " Pilgrim's Progrese " but there were no clerics. The difference between the cleric and the minister wal that the cleric invariably steed on hie dignity ; whilet the nolaister had to stand on hie legs. (Laughter.) The lecturer was cordielly thanked on the propeeition of the Rev. C H Hocken, seconded by Mr E J Guest.

Mr B Moreton presided at the open meeting ef tke abeam society which was held in the Free Ddethodiit Cnurch cm Sunday. Tha speaker wag Mr R Wood. liaise Sumner very pleasingly rendered the soles " I rested nigh an old ehurch door "and "Glory to Thee my God, this night." Miss Ethel %sett was equally effective in her rendition of " Join, !Over of my seal "1 and " Cast thy breed upon the waters." The Chairmen said he had been impressed with the thought that the P.S.A. had not a very comprehensive title, although it had a vary, very comprehensive object Some men end women looked upon the pleasant Sunday afternoon as a mere passing pleasure, but that, geld the Chairomen,wes not true. It get men and women to understand their spiritual coudition. Mr Wood based his address upon " The Bible," in the course of which he said he liked the Bible beoause it was the best book he had ever read, If they took it as a piece of literature, no book could go beyond its diction. It contained histeric accounts that could not be equalled in any ether book. Be loved che Bible because it was mere than a beak ef history, of poetry, or drama. It was tha only book wherein Gad communicated with man. No other book could take the place of the Bible in coming into direct contact with God and man. Even the sinner would go to the Bible In time of trouble, and find solace an i comfort. To understand the Bible one must learn sennethine ef its Watery.

div.p: MYSTERIES OF THE EAR.

In a late number of the "Journal for the Deaf," there is a aeries of popular articles describing the anatomy and physiology of the ear, and the various ways of be- coining deaf. This publication which is devoted entirely to the interests of those who are affliotml by deafness, or by any diseases of the ear, nose, or throat, can be obtained free by post by addressing the Secretary, Dreuet Inotitute, Regent's-park-road, Primrose-bill,Lsn- don, N.W. The" Journal" also describes a Method of Treating deafness by external application that has teen repeatedly successful is curinz ear diseases and in rester log hearing in cases pronounced incurable by the usual aural treatment. Those who are interested in knowing how to apply this method will Cad that each" Journal" is accompanied by a Patient's Report Form, which en- ables anyone t receive full particulars as to the use of thf treattnant at horn,. Any advice by correspondence is absolutely free.

The Manchester and Liverpool District Bank- ing Company, Ltd. The report of the directors of this banking com- pany has been issued and will be presented at the meeting of shareholders to be held on the 16th of July. The directors report that the gross profit for the half-year ending 30th June last, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, is £226,216 Is 7cl, to which has to be added the amount brought forward from 31st December last, viz ;—£30,356 7e 3d, mak- ing a total of £256 572 8s 10d. From this sum.the following deductions have to be made :—Total ex- penses at the head office,London office,end branches, including 'salaries, stationery, taxes. &c, £75,755 58 10d; half year's provision for income tax, £6,500, leaving a net profit of £171,317 as. The directors recommend the declaration of a dividend ofi 15s a share. and bonus of 5s a share, which will take £125.000, leaving a balance of £46,317 as. Of this it is proposed to carry to the reserve fund, £15,000 and to next account, £31,317 3s. The reserve fund, with the above addition, will then amount to £2,090,000.
BEEORE the MAGISTRATES

A CONTEMPTIBLE FRAIND—TRADING oN PATRIOTIC SENTIMENT. At the Warrington Police Court on Friday, before the Deputy-Mayor and other magistrates, Tnomas Wilson, a stranger to the town, was charged on remand with obtaining alms by false pretences in Bold-street on June 24th.— Supesintendent Monaghan said the prisoner went to the house of Mr Williams, 10, Bold-street. and told Mr Williams that he had been sent there by Dr Smith. He stated that he had been out at the front, and hal been wounded in four places, and his wife and family were starving. He was wearing the South African ribbon, and in consideration of 13,3 statement Mr Williams gave him sixpence. The same afternoon Mr Williams saw the man in Bridge Street under the influence of drink with his arm in a sling, and the matter was reported to the police. Twe days afterwards prisoner came to him (Snperintendent Monaghan) and said he had lost his army Papers. He (the Superintendent) invited him into the Police Station, and prisoner told him that he was in South Africa during the whole of the war, He (the Suoerintendent)replied " It speaks well for you." He then sent for Mr Williams,who identified prisoner as the man who visited him. Prisoner subsequently said he had been In the army but admitted that he had never been to the front.—The Chair nen said the prisoner saw him and told him that he was a discharged yeoman and. had been to the front. He also stated that he had reaelved orders to go to Loudon for the Coronation and would be paid 16s per day.—The Chairman said that the offence, making use of the patriotic sentiment of the people for the purpose for which prisoner had tried to make use of it, deserved the fail penalty the law could impose. People had quite enough to do to help those who really deserved help and had done that which justified it, but scamps like the prisoner, who traded on his feeling, de- served the maximum nenaltv.—Prisener said he had been to the front and could prove it.—The magistrates com- mitted. him to gaol for three months.—Prisoner : I wish you could give ma twelve,—The Chairman : I wish we could.

div.head: MINOR OASES.
div.p: MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.
SATURDAY. —Before Meimrs W Hayward (in the chair) and
Id Thornton.

TNIEP SENT TO Giant -James Shields. Stanley-street, was charged with stealing a erab from Maguire's oyster shop in linttermarket-street on Wednesday evening; also with stealing a wiaker haadbasket of th- value of 2s 6,1 fr urn the shop of Sam N Green, Market-place, maid further with steel- ing a metal alarm clock of the value of 7s 6d from the house of Frederick Brooks, in Winwlsk-street on the same day.— Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner went to the oyster slop and purchased some oysters. When he left the shop he was seen by P.O Howard to t4re a crab. The officer , followed him down an entry and brought him back. He took him into custody and the prisoner then said it was all a mistake as the" crab caught hold of his finger." He was brought before the Court and remanded for inquiries to be made, as he had a metal clock in his possession at the time. This, it was found had been stolen from a dwelling-house in Winwisk-street. It was also ascertained that a basket had been missed from outside Mr Green's shop on Wednesday, land that the prissier had sold it far 21 in Mersey-street.— The prisoner, who said he was drunk at the time, was sent to ' gaol for 28 days, ILLTREATING A HORSE.—John Smith, last from Man- chester, was charged with ill-treating a horse, by travelling it while in an unit state, en the 28th of June —P.-. Millington proved the ease and said he saw the horse in flanshester-road about midnight. It was lame and suffer- ing minalderablv.—lnspeetor Print said he examined the animal, which was lame in both fore legs from ring bone and contracted tendons.—The defendant, who consented to sell the horse to be killed, was ordered to pay the coats__

BRINGING BEFR INTO THE WORICHOURE.—JOhn Platt, an inmate of the Workhouse, was charged with unlawfully taking into the Workhouse a bottle of be.r —Mr Gates, the master, said that on Tuesday night the prisoner went out to post some letters, and returned In a quarter of an hour with the bottle of beer. It was found on him by an officer, who caught him in the act of cmsuming it.—This was prisOner's 9th appea ranee, and he was sent to gaol for 21 days. MONDAY—Before Messrs F Monks (in the chair), Meehan Hayward,Thornton and Wright. RUFFIANLY CONDUCr.—ThoMas Cassidy, no fixed abode, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at twenty minutes past ten on Saturday night, and also with assaulting William Arthur Roberts in Chester-road' H pleaded guilty to aeing drunk, but denied all knowledge of the assault.— Superintendent Monaghan said Mr Roberts was a commercial traveller, who lived in Prescot. lie was walking along Cheater-road on Saturday night in the direction of War- rington In company with a young lady, when they met prisoner coming in the opposite direction under the influence of drink. Prisoner (rune up to Mr Roberts, who was a smal man compared with him, and, seizing him by the coat collar he said, "You are the man I want some money from." M Roberts told him he had none for him. whereupon he said he must have some. The lady at this point saw Police-con- stable Millington, and prisoner theu went away. The officer followed, and t ok him into custody. The place where the aft sir occurred was a very quiet part, and had the offieer not come on the scene something serious might have occurred.—The bench committed prisoner to goal for on month.

A DRUNKEY FRRAIC. —James Allan Kelly, 4, Pitt-street, was charged with being found in the dwelling-house of Elizabeth Smith, 4. Wakefield-street,at twenty minutes past twelve on Sunday morning, with intent to commit a felony. —Police-constable Hewitt said that shortly after twelve o'clock he received certain information, and went to 4,Wake- field-street. He had to climb over the yard ga,e, and then saw the prisoner looking round the kitchen with alighted candle. When asked what he was doing there, he said he had been asksd. to light the fire. No one else was in the house,•as Mra Smith was at her daughter's. The back kitchen window was broken. Prisoner was taken to the police station.—Prisoner admitted being in the house, but said he was under the influence of drink. He was a great friend of the family, and be went to see the son. He broke the window by catching his foot against the yard brush, which fell against the glass. He would not have done anything of the kind had he not had some drink.—The bench considered that that the case was really a drunken freak and that there was no felonious intent. They advised prisoner to keep clear of drink, and discharged him on payment of costs. affronT HAVE BE,CIP Szarous.—Robert Martin, Long-lane, Orford, was summoned for leaving his heree unattended in Regent-street on June 28th.—P 9 Evans stated that on the date in question, Walking Day,the horse was left unattended at the time when the procession was taking place. When witness saw it it was beginning to runaway, and If it had not been stopped it would no doubt have dashed into the children in Sankey-street It appeared that defendant had been in the "White Hart" hotel.—Defenoant who said that all was quiet when he left the horse, was fined 10s.
TUE3o.l.Y.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hutchinson, and Dr Fox,

THEFT OF BOOTS AND SHOES.—Albert Hincheliffe, Cloth Hall-yard, was charged with stealing from the shop of J N Brown and Company three pairs of cycling shoes, of the value of 14s 9d, on Monday afternoon, and 'further with stealing a pair of army boots, of the value of 4s 3d, from the shop of Baker and Son. Horsemarket-street, on Saturday night. He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Monaghan said that at three o'clock on Monday afternoon the assistant at Messrs Brown's, Annie Jones, heard the noise of shoes knocking against the window. She looked through the window and saw the prisoner making away with the shoes and the ticket. She followed him and gave information to the police, and prisoner was arrested by Sergeant Bell. When taken to the Police Station he admitted having taken the shoes. On Saturday night at eight o'clock, Mr Albert rritehard, manager for Mr Baker, saw a pair of army boots safe outside the shop and an hour later they were missing. He reported the matter to the police and inquiries were made without success. On Monday afternoon he (the superin- tendent)went to the prisoner's lodging-house and ascertained that he had offered a pair of boots for sale on Saturday night similar to those missed by Mr Pritchard. He did not sell them that night, but sold them the next morning to a man on the road for 3s. The man went away shortly after Prisoner was sent to gaol for fourteen days on each cbarg

div.p: FOR IHE SOLDIERS.

Opening of a Club at Warrington. Along felt want in Warringcon will be supplied by the opening of the Soidiers' Club in Bawsey-road. Hitherto there has beeu ne place apscially eet apart for soldiers and volunteers to spend their leisure hours, but last week Major General Hallam. Pair, C. 8., commanding toe Nerth-Westero dis- trict, opened a club at which there is ample Provision for the enjoyment or wholesale recreation by r,?gular soldiers, mili'3irimen, and volunteers. 'The Inovement for the establishment of the club was initiated by Colonel E H Fitzberbert, commanding the Bth and 40th regimental districts, and his efforts have received cordial support from members of the local regiments and also from many townspeople. One object Which Colonel Fit zuerbert had in veiw was to provide a memorial of the South African Campaign, and it Will be agreed that the memorial takes a very appropriate form. The club premises are at tke house formerly occupied by Mr Ziba Armitage and slabsequently by Mr El Milliog, Mr T Pilkington and Dr Adams, and the building is in every way adapted for the puroose for which it will be used, the rooms being large, lofty, well lighted and airy. It has been carefully pt-papered and painted and the walls hung with pic- tures. On the left on entering is the game loom, where have been provided a semi-billiard table, chess, draughts and dominoes. Near it is what is called the " Silent Room," in other words the library for writing and re ading, in which will be placed panels hearing the names of the Lancashire officers and men who died from wounds or disease during the war. The library is well stocked with books—fiction, poetry, biography, theology, and travel being well represented—and the selection is as varied as it well can be. Another room contain the coffee bar and tables for light refreshments but no intoxicants will be supplied. Upstairs are the conatnittee room, bathroom, bedrooms, news room, a reception room for sergeants and their frieads, and:a tOOM in which those fond of ping-pong can enjoy them" selves to the full. Sergeant George Blake, who has recently returned from South Africa, where he has been cri active service for about two years, is acting as toanager and caretaker of the premises. Despite the uafavourable weather a large cumber of ne, wnspeople assembled to witness the opening ceremony. ..‘,1113 band from the Barracks was in attendance and elaVed several selections in a very creditable manner. A Platform had been erected on the footpath, and from it aPeeches were delivered. Amongst those present were the Mayor and Mayoress and Miss Parr, Col. Fitzherbert aecd officers of the 8/40th Regimental District, Colonel bzfidgesay, Major Rooms, and officers of the 2sc V.B. ;AV.V. (South Lancashire Regiment),the Deputy Mayor qdderman Roberts), and several members of the Towu e c4uncil, the Rector of Warrington and Mrs Willis, and Other ladies and gentlemen. . In opening the proceedings, Colonel FITZHCHBERT Aid it was a very great pleasure to him to be able to tedeena the pledge that was given a little more than a tier ago to the Service Company when they were going the front. That pledge was made at a dinner at the cena Hall when the Deputy-Mayor presided. Alder- ..:lan Roberts gave his support to the scheme for the PrOvision of a club for the soldiers of the line, militia, ;310(1 volunteers, and he the speaker) promised to do his ,„eilt to have the club ready for use when the Service es'coapany returned from the front. Everything was ready for the opening, and at six o'clock that even- 'eg 'volunteers, soldiers, and militia would be free to lilts the club. The only part that was not complete was ue: memorial cbamber to these who bad fallen in the Zarr, and whieh would contain the names of those who ad died in South Africa. It was a long task, and it ,fle ...was in the hands of an old soldier in the town who was ;ell known to them—Mr Dell— who was taking a deep .s'aterest in the work, and he was sure that when it was up they would all be very pleased with the inscrip- -11•24. FTe could not repeat the names of the men, but y could repeat the heading at the top :—" Roll of `4ocsshire soldiers who died in the South African cam- paign 1899 to 1902. They died, they fell, some by Zealot's, some by disease, but all died for the honour of eir country, their regiment, and their King." (Ap- plause.) Major-tieneral HALLikat PAttn, in the course of his ePeecn, said he wished to make the acquaintance of the people of Warrington, and it always afforded him great Pleasure to have anything to do with a soldiers' club. The territorial regiments must be indebted to Colonel Pitzherbert for the energy and tact he had shown in establishing the club. It was a very fine one and well crorthy of all support. He understood that not only the territorial regiments had borne their proportion of the rlrPenditure. but a large proportion had been locally anbseribed. That was very gratifying in many ways and showed the kindly feeling and sympathy with /ettioh soldiers were regarded in Warrington. He banked the Mayor for so kindly giving them his Cou ndntenance on that cecasion,a he had, in conclusion, tp declare the club open and to wish it all success. Applause,) The sign board, which had been covered with a cloth, *as then unveiled amid arplause, and the band played 1411:erSs of" God cave the King." The Union Jack was °Med on the flag staff in the club grounds. mavoa'eheri delivered a brief speech in which he rlid feel that we owe a debt of gratitude te Col. tzherbert for originating and carrying out this scheme :lid this brings me to contemplate another, and less side of our picture, for I fear we cannot can- ceal from ourselves, that we are on the eve of parting L"ith our kind, genial, and sociable friend Co!. Fitz- "ether% As Mayor of Warrington I wish to take this ;Priortunity of Bayne, how much we are indebted to him .2r the unvarying consideration and generous assistance we have always received at his hands, and for his e°,4lial and energetic co-operation, in all matters ia Zeraich the military authorities and the Corporation have Len jointly concerned. (Applause.) I feel we cannot Ftter express our thanks and appreciation to the e Ilonel that by supporting and assisting him in the ticrnee be has so much at heart,and I rejoice to feel that e kind presence of General 13allam Parr, who has t coe us the honour of paying his first visit to Warring- to open this club to-iay, will give it an honourable f`:art and be a hippy augury for its future success. his ‘'einel fuse. ) concluded the opening preceedings,and the visitors trrPeceed the interior of the club. Major-Genera 1 e allarn-Parr expressed himself well satisfied with 411 the angemente which had been made for the aecoMmOda- len of the soldiers.

THE MAYOR AND THE POSTPONE- MENT OF THE CELEBRATIONS. The Mayor has addressed the following letter to the Chief Constable. Dear Sir,—Now that the memorable and moment- ous week is over I wish to express to you my satis- faction as Mayor of our County Borough at the admir- Male order and good conduct which have prevailed during this trying time. I do not think it possible for any;town to have passed through these exceptional circumstances more credit- ably than Warrington has done, and I consider we could not have paid a more pathetic tribute to our stricken and suffering King than we did in the calm ialld dignified resignation of our people when the cup of *s°olr the place of rej°Y was dashed from their lips and-Anxiety and doubt °icing, and merry making. ' It was with a grave feeling of responsibility that our e'tncutive decided to abandon the preparations for the onation celebrations and I feel very grateful that action was rightly consttued and so loyally iniesced in by the Procession Committee and the ne rk,l ndly societies and others whom they represented. , • I,tWithstanding the disappointment and loss it 7.vitably occasioned. 44' feel proud that all have co-operated so cordially in d.Porting me and tiding me over a period of much 'nculty.—i am, yours faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR, lawn Mayor. Hall, July Ist, 1902.

div.head: ) THE TRAMWAYS,
div.p: ) THE TRAMWAYS,
The Position of Stockton Heath,
Interview with Alderman Roberts. Small Cheer for the `‘ Heathens."

A reporter of the "Examiner" waited upon Alder- man Roberts the chairman of the Tramways Com- mittee with the object of gaining further informa- tion with reference to the position of Stockton Heath and the tramway system. Our readers will remember that in the early part of the year the Corporation applied to the Light Railway Com- missioners for an order to construct a loop line from the tramway terminus at Stafford-road, Wilderspool, to Victoria :'quare,Stockton Heath,and thence along Orappenhall-road to the Latchford terminus of the tramway system. The Stock- ton Heath Parish Council at once sub- mitted terms for the acceptance of the Corporation. The Corporation were unable to comply with everything asked for but the follow- ing terms were agreed to :—That only electric power be used except with the consent of not only the Board of Trade, but also the Local Authority. That the words "and local "be added between road and authority in line 2, page 6. That positions and levels of lines should be approved by the road and local authorities. That the space between the rails and 8 inches on the outside of such rails be paved with setts; that the rails be the same design weight and construction as are now used by the dorpora- tion on their tramways; that where any tele- graph or telephone or other wire or wires cross over the wires of the railway the same be protected from contact with such electric wires. _ _ _

The following further conditions were submitted, but not agreed to :—That Old London-road be widened to at least 50 feet, the metalled portion being, say 35 feet and that two lines of rails be affixed; that except with the consent of the road and local authorities the line be used for passenger traffic only, and that the agreement for running powers with the Northwieh Light Railway be for passenger traffic only, except with a like consent. That the following be inserted," provided that not more than one penny be charged for the journey between Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, and Rylands-strett, Warrington " ; that the Corporation light the roads on which the railway is to run. The Stockton Heath Parish Council was not satisfied with the terms agreed to and opposed the application of the Corporation b3fore the Light Railway Commissioners. They persisted in their demand for road widenings. penny fares and the lighting of the roads by the Corporation and it is upon the conditions imposed by the Light Railway Order that a deadlock has taken place.

Our reporter asked Alderman Roberts, the nature of the conditions which have been imposed on the Corporation. In reply, the Alderman said they included the widening of Old London-road to such an extent that the Corporation, if they accepted the Order, would be obliged to purchase a ;block of property opposite the Mulberry Tree Inn and another block opposite St Thomas's Church, besides smaller zoncessions elsewhere. Not only were the roads to be widened at the expense of the Corpora- tion, but the Corporation must light the roads on which the trams run. The order imposed a condi- tion upon the Corporation of lighting every pole whether in the middle or side of the road,and conse- quently there would be no necessity for the Stock- ton Heath authority to pay the Corporation fo.l lighting their roade,as they did at the present time. "And what will be the extra cost of carrying out these onerous conditions 5" "It will be, as I stated in the Council Chamber this week, at least double .the price we have paid fir the same length of line in Warrington Then it must also be remembered that there will be an additional annual charge for the cost of signalling and conducting the traffic over the swing bridge which crosses the Ship Canal." "Owing to the restriction to a penny fare to Victoria &quare, 1 suppose you do not anticipate any additional revenue for this extra expenditure?, "Well we shall shortly be receiving a penny fare for conveying passengers to Stafford-road, and the only income we could expect from the construction of the line to Victoria Square would be the additional traffic which the longer linewould bring." 6' Do you think the Corporation will undertake the risk under such conditions ?" " As business men, we are not likely to construct a line without there is a prospect of an adequate return. The Stockton Heath Parish Council has been ill-advised in driving too hard a bargain. They have really cut their noses off to spite their faces. "1 suppose you think the Stockton Heath Parish Council has been endeavouring to get advantages possessed by urban authorities at the expense of.,the Warrington ratepayers ?" " That is so and a little more be‘ildes. If we carried out the order, they would get a road straightened ,and widened at our expense, they would get it lighted for nothing, and they would get the tramway system extended to Victoria- square without an extra fare being charged. I think they will find they have over-reached them- selves. A quick tramway service to Victoria-square would in itself have been a desirable acquisition for a rising suburb like Stockton Heath and it would have, been to their advantage to have met the Corporation in a more liberal spirit."
Liverpool Volunteers at Warrington,

The composite company of the Liverpool Volun- teers, made up of the Ist, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th and 7th Battalions ot the Liverpool Regiment, arrived at the Central Station from the front on Monday evening. A large number of friends and relatives of the men had journeyed from Liverpool, and I heartily greeted the returned warriors as they de- trained. The men, who looked in the best of con- dition, numbered 38, and were under the command of Captain Ilignett and Lieutenants Cohen and Buckley. They were lined up outside the station, land, headed by the band of the depot, marched to the barracks, followed by an enthusiastic crowd. The men have put in months' services in South Africa.—An exciting scene was witnessed as the men arrived at the station. A man and woman, probably visitors, jumped on to the metals to cross the line to the opposite platform, but failed to notice the approach of the Manchester train. A gentleman on ths platform just managed to pull the woman out of danger and the man also had a very narrow escape. Thekrain dashed past as they reached the platform.—The Volunteers left the Central Station on Tuesday evening at 7.45 by special train for Liverpool. The band accompanied them to the station, and as they were entraining Played "Soldiers of the King." The train steamed off to the strains of "Auld lang syne," and a large crowd assembled in the street raised hearty cheers. Warrington P.S.A. Society.

At the meeting of this Society on Sunday after- noon the quarterly prize distribution to members for regular attendance took place. Mr Ellison was the chairman,and he filled the few minutes allotted to him admirably. Mr Ciregson gave a sound evan- gelical address, which was thoroughly enjoyed The so!oist for the occasion was Mr H. Taylor, who was well received. Prayer was offered by Mr Taker, and the Scripture lesson was read by Mr Clegg, the service concluding with the Benediction,

div.head: Poor Boys' Camp.
div.p: Poor Boys' Camp.

On Monday 88 poor boys left the Central Station for the Boy,' Summer Camp, Birkdale, where they will remain until Monday morning. The expenses are being kindly defrayed by Mr Arthur H Lee, who each year makes this outing his special hobby. The School Attendance Offizes, Bank House, have been besieged each day by en eager crowd of youngsters anxious to participate in the visit, and everal disappointed ones asked that their names should be put down for nest year, 80 that they could be in time.

div.head: REV. C. FINQH. Departure from Warrington.
div.p: THE REV. C. FINQH. Departure from Warrington.
FAREWELL MEETING.

A meeting was held in Legh-street chapel on Thursday last week, for the purpose of bid- ding farewell to the Rev C Finch. There was a large attendance, over which Mr Griffiths presided. Continuing. the CHAIRMAN said they were met to express their love and regard for Mr Finch, who was leaving them for a new sphere of Christian labour. There was, he believed, general regret at Mr Finch's removal. Felbw-townsmen whom he (the speakcr) had met had paid sincere tributes of their regard and esteem for Mr Finch, and even those in the town who were not conhected with any Christian Church thought be was a most conscientious and atleChristian minister. Ha left them in a spirit of perfect harmony. He would leave no jarring string, and rim wounds to heal, but he would leave a united church, stronger in many respects than when he entered upon his ministry. The result of his labours was to be seen in the encouraging state of the Church, the Sunday School, and the Christian En- deavour Society. The congregation bad also increased, and there was an improvement in the financial condition of the church. They were very sorry indeed at Mr Finch's removal from their midst. In conclusion he wished Mr and Mrs Finch every success in their new sphere of about. _ _ .

Speeches were then delivered by Mr Swales,the oldest local preacher, (representing the trustees), Mr Bissell, (representing the Sunday School), Mr Barrett (repre- senting the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour), and Mr Metcalf (Latchford). The Rev Join; YONGE was the next speaker. He said he could say most frankly that few ministers who had come into the town since he (the speaker) came, had so completely commended themselves to the general esteem of their brethren as Mr Finch had done. The local ministers would be very sorry to lose him, and they would follow him with affection and sympathy and with the best wishes for his succas in Congleton or any where else that God's Providence might lead him. The Rev T BISHOP referred to Mr Finch'e kindliness and geniality, and said he had always beard people in the town speak in the very highest -terms of Mr Pinch. He wiehed him every prosperity and happiness in his new sphere. The Revs J P MATTHEWS, C H HOCZEN, and J W WADDELL (Widnes) also spoke in terms of appreciation of Mr Finch's work. In reply the Rev C FINCH said he had simply tried to do his duty. He was very grateful to the triends who lead spoken for their words of stimulus and encourage- Ment. Continuing the rev gentleman tendered his hearty thanks to those among whom he had worked for the past six years,for all the kindness they had extended o him. He should carry into his new sphere of labour he most pleasant reminiscences of his work in Warring- ton, and he was glad to know that be was going away ivith the affectionate remembrance of his Warrington friends. The speaker proceeded to ochort his hearers to do their utmost for the welfare of the church. Sunday school, and Christian Endeavour. He hoped that in the near future they would have a batter House of Prayer than that. He did not think that that etlitice and its situation were what they ought to have hi a town like this. In conclusion he expieesed the hope that the church would be a strong church and a power for good in the town. 4 hymn having been sung the meeting concluded with the Benediction.

A Warrington Child's Sad Death.

Mr S Brighouse, County Coroner, conducted an inquest at tha Coroner's Court on Monday evening, touching the death of Stanley Webb, the 13 months old child of Arthur and Frances Harriet Webb, 94, Bostock-street, who died on the previous Friday from blood poisoning.—Deceased's mother stated that the child was with her in the kitchen at ten o'clock on Friday morning, May 16th. Witness was cleaning the fire grate and the hearth, when a small hot cinder fell out of the grate. 'Deceased, who was close to, put his hand on the cinder, which caused a slight burn. Witness dressed it, and in a few days it appeared to be better, but on the 13th June he became worse, and Dr Naden was rant for. He came to the house, and said the deceased was suffer- ing from blood-poisoning set up by the burn. He attended deceased until his death, which took place lon Fri Jay afternoon last.—The Coroner explained to the jury that it was necessary to hold an inquest, as the certificate disclosed the feet that the death was other tban from natural causes.—A ver- dict of" Accidental death" was returned.

The Approaching Marriage of Miss S. Reynolds. An interesting ceremony took place at the Stam- ford Estates Office, Altrincham, last Friday, when a deputation representing the tenantry of the Cheshire estate belonging to the trustees of the late Earl of , Stamford and Warrington met for the purpose of presenting a valuable piece of plate to Mr William ' Douglas Bullock, J.P., the popular and respected agent of the trust ees,the occasion being that of his approaching marriage with Miss S Reynolds, daughter of the :late Captain Reynolds, J.P., of .'..atchford. The presentation took the form; of a massive solid silver salver of beautiful design,there being engraved upon the centre of it Mr Bullock's family crest and coat of arms. The deputation con- sisted of Messrs G P Noden (Yew Tree) and Thomas Winstanley (Little Heath), of Dunham Massey, and Messrs William Speakman (Carrington Hall) end G H Newton (The Ackers), of Carrington, the presentation being made by the latter gentle- man in the absence (through ill-health) of Mr John Collins, or Carrington, who is the oldest tenant on the estate.—Several members of the deputation delivered appropriate speeches, and Mr Bullock briefly replied.

RUNCORN COTTAGE HOSPITAL.

div.head: Sir John T._ Brunner Lays the
div.p: Sir John T._ Brunner Lays the
Foundation Stone:

At last the foundation stone of the Runcorn Cottage I Hospital has been laid. Over twenty years ago the old Board of Commissioners considered the question, bin owing to financial reasons3he echeme had to be aban- dened. Since that time repeated efforts have been made to float a cottage hospital scheme, but without avail, and it was left to the Runcorn Cycle Club to really lay the foundation stone ot the present enterprise. Through parade@ and private and public subscription they raised some £4OO towards the scheme which really formed the nucleus of £1,600 which has now been subscribed for the purpose. The estimated cost of the erection is £2,000 and there is no doubt but the balance -will be torthcoming ere long. The site that has been chosen is an excellent one and central to the chief works. The building will have three wards with eight beds, then there will be three bedrooms, kitchens upstairs and downstairs, an operating room, &c., and will no doubt be a model building. Toe architect, who has given his services, is Mr James Wilding (surveyor to the Council),l and the contractor is Mr W Nickson, of Runcorn. Saturday saw the first important step taken towards 1 the erection of the building. At 530 the members of I the Council with the Runcorn Cycle Ulub and the St ' John's Ambulance Association formed the procession at the Town Hall and beaded by the Volunteer band marched to the hospital site. Awaiting their arrival was a huge crowd who greeted them with hearty cheers as Sir John Brunner, who bad arrived a few minutes previously, joined Mr Taylor and his colleague,. Among others present were :—Messrs R fl Posnett, J Pritchard, E Imison, T Jones, D Bisbrown, H J Grice, S Walton, G H Kirkham, and J J Sbaw ; Mr E Marshall (secretary t the Council), Mr W Jones (assistant secretary), Mr J Wilding (surveyor and architect), Mr G Barker (con- sulting surveyor to the Council), Mr J Percival (sani- tary inspector), the Revs S T Morris, and A Wells, and Messrs F J Norman, AR Norman, T Jones,Dr McLennan. W Hankinson, Jlt Frith, A Lightburn, J M Frith, J Douglas, T La, S Pope, A Riley and J Johnson, Rm. The inscription on the atone was " This foundation stone was laid by Sir J T Brunner, Bart., M.P., July sth. 1902." . _

I The proceedings having been commenced with the singing of the National Anthem, Mr S Taylor, after paying a high tribute to the worth of Sir John Brunner, who had always proved himself ready to help any good cause said they had been struggl- ing hard for something like eight or ten years to raise funds with the object of accomplishing what they were there that night to do, and he might say that during those years the working people of Runcorn themselves had taken a very deep interest in the work. Their friends, the Cycle Club Committee, had year by year determinedly helped the work forward by holding their parades, and he was told that up to that time they had raised over £4OO. (Hear, bear, and applause.) That, he might say, was practically subscribed by the work- ing people themselves. They had now, he thought, up to that day funds amounting to about L 1,600 —(hear, hear)—thanks to Sir John Brunner and others whose names they would know. Sir John himself had promised them a splendid donation of £2OO. (Hear, hear.) Ttey were still something like £4OO or £5OO short of bat was required to erect the building and equip it, but he felt sure, looking round upon the large number that by their presence showed that they were interested, that they might well hope to raise the balance at no very distant date. He was sure that the people of Runcorn would do all in their power to help forward the move- ment.

Mr James Wilding then handed a silver and ivory trowel to Sir John Brunner, Mr Wiswall presenting a mallet. The trowel was suitably inscribed and the pre- sentation was appropriately acknowledged. Sir Jonn Brunner then said that Mr Taylor had spoken to them of the good work that the Cycle Club had done in relation to that hospital and he was glad to praise them as he had watched the work they had done from the small beginning. It was now several years ago since they held the first parade which, in the first instance, realized something like £6O. (Hear, hear). They had stuck to that work like men and the fruit of their labour and the labour of those who had also interested them- selves in the good work was that they had a very goodly sum with which to begin the building of that hoe pital (Hear, hear). Following the example of the Cycle Club many a good man, and several, he hoped of the ladies of Runcorn, had in a self-denying spirit put their haede in their pockets and given in aid of the scheme. Mr Taylor had Said to them that there were many there be- fore them that evooine who woul I in time to come realise in person or through those near and dear to them the good wcrk that hospital was intended to do, and he commended it to them all, to the trade unions, to those in co•operative societies, and be hoped that they would give not out of their abundance, but out of the narrowness of their means. He had come as they knew from London. where in Parliament, they were eneaged in the consideration of a Bill introduced by the Government that was fraught with very great good to the people of this country in time to come. He meant the Education Bill. neat Bill would bring in the future what was to his mind a large difference. Hereafter the County Councils and the Urban Ceuncill would have all the powers possessed up to that time by the School Boards and be would call to their recol;ection. and tell to those who had hitherto not known it, that the London School:Board and many an- other board,but the London School Board pre-eminently had atten•ed Cr' the children's eyes, ear 3, and teeth. Under the eew (vier he hoped to see the Cheshire County Council foremost in setting a good example by taking up this work of attending to the children's eyes, ears, and teeth. (epplauee)l This would prevent many and many a child growing up into an inefficient citizen and would make each child, by tending one after another, a much rno-e efficient citizen—than that child could pose- iblylotherwhe become. If there were any member of the County Council there. he hoped, he would see to it that before many months had passed a prorneralshould.bemade to the Cheshire County Council to take up this work—a work godlike in its nature—and that it would be under- taken on their behalf and on behalf of the whole country. Every child that they made more efficient, every cripple they helped in that building, every wounded soldier of industry who came there and was fitted for life again, paid them over and over again the amount that was spent upon him. (Applause.) It was indeed an econ- omical work that they had undertaken that day. He did not think they would corsider him impertinent if he tendered to them and the gentlemen around him upon that platform a piece of advice, namely,that that build- ing and the land upon which it was set, should he held in trust inc them by the representatives of them all, the Urban District Council. If the present trustees banded it over ,o the Council, it would be with an understand- ing on the part of the trustees, and aa understanding on the part of those who accepted it, the Urban Council, that they would hold it as one of the highest duties to attend and ameliorate the suffering in the interests of the public health and well-being. (Hear, hear.) The undertaking that they were inaugurating together, was one in which be was delighted to participate, and a work that was fostered by the noblest impulses that God had put into the heart of man. It was in that feeling of high hope and in the sense that it was a work that had God's blessing upon it, that he would lay the foundation stone of the new building. (Applause.) Sir Jelin then laid the stone, declaring it to be " well and truly laid "amidst rounds of cheers. In the cavity of the stone he placed a sealed bottle containing current issues of the three local papers, a copy of the " Liver- pool Courier " and an account of the ceremony written by Mr Wilding, associating with it the name of Mr S Taylor, as Chairman of the Council, and Sir John Brunner'e name also.
Votes of thanks brought tloP ceremony to a close, the procession subsequently re-forming and marching back to the Town He.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH
FINANCE. The Corporation Balance Sheet.

We have been furnished with a copy of the accounts of the Corporation of Warrington. issued by Mr John Fairhurst, F.S.A.A. (Borougn Treasurer) for the year ended 31st Marcia last. It is a bulky volume of over 200 pages, and contains a mass of information relative to tue financial positson of the Borough. THE BALaNCE SHEET. Accompanying the accouats is an aggregate balance sheet of the 16 biiities and assets of the Corporation. The total liabilities are set forth as amounting to £974,630 us 13, and the assets £1,321,963 Ils 13, thus showing a balance of assets amounting to £347,333. The particulars of this balance sheet show the liabilities and assets in connection with tne following full& : Borough rate fund, liabilities, £66,167 4s 61 ; assets, £142,981 193 71 ; improvement rate iund, liabilities, £226,137 ; assets, £307,682 17s 83 ; sewers rate, liabiiities. £34,395 63 20 ; assets, , £63,868 89 31 • gas works, liabditir.s. £190,538 93 ; I assets, £290,93993 31 ; water works, liabilities,£34B,l9s 93 33 ' • assets,£3B2,o92 33 103 • electricity, liabilities, I £52,886 159 24 ; assets, £51,74'9 14s 21 ; tramways, liabilities, £39.980 18s • assets, £39,419 53 ; Parr Hall, liabilities, £733 133 103 ; assets, £8,973 is 73 ; private improvement expenses,liabilities and assets,£ls,s9s 153 24; picture purchase,assets, £607 33 9 1; Latcnford and Wilderspool Causeways, assets, £3,171 193 ; Middleton scholarships. assets, £1,048 14s 23 ; Walker's gilt, assets, £587 7s ; police superannuation, assets. £12,974 183 id ; fire engine renewal fund, assets, £270 14s 63. div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
The Corporation and Disputes.
The monthly meeting of the Warriturron Trades and Labour Council was held at the Druids' Hall on Tuesday evening, Mr T Edwardson presiding over a fair attend- ance..
CORPOSS.TION DISPUTES.-•THS TOWN COUNCIL'S RESOLU-
TION NOT SATISFACTORY.
The SECRETARY t :ad a letter from the Town Clerk enclosing ; .he resoluticu passed by the Town Council lat week wito st-lerclice to disputes and official intervention.

The CHAIIMAN contended that! the Trades Council's original resolution ought to stand good. The SECRETARf eaid there was not the slightest possible chance ot getting the Town Council to adopt the original resolution. Either they must have the Town Council's resolution or none at all. He did not think the resolution would be of much use to them but at the same time be did not think it would be possible, with the Corporation as at present coustitoted,to obtain a better one. Be suggested that they accept the resolution for the present, and take further steps when favourable opportunity presented itself. Without a doubt the men had been treated shabbily in the past, despite what Alderman Robert said. He hoped that in the future they might get men of wider views on the Council.

Mr YORKE considered the resolution was fairly satis- factory for a start. Mr HAMBLETT did not agree with the resolution, but thought it would be best to accept it for the time being. He considered that the discourtesy which was shown to Councillor Evans at the Council meeting was very un- gentlemanly. One Alderman above all others, seemed to take a delight in this Mr Bucxr.ny said the remarks of Alderman Sutton were very unfair, not only to Councillor Evans but also to the Trades Council. It seemed to be treating the coun- cil wit., a great deal of contempt—contempt which they did not deserve, and which' they were not going to stand. It was time the Council made a move in these matters, and if they could prove cases in which men had been badly treated by the Corporation, to prove them and bring them forward and show the public what had been done. The resolution adopted by the Council was not one iota better than the present conditions ; in his opinion it was worse. The Corporation wanted the men to come before the sub-committees so that they would know who were the ring-leaders, and could make) scape-goats of them. They could not make a seape-goat of a Trade Union official Iveause be stood in an independent position. The men had not the debating powers to discuss these matters. He was of the opinion that the Council ought to mkae another attempt to get Councillor Evans to move this resolution, and it possible, they could find out the men who voted against it, and appeared to be their enemies, and treated them with contempt, Mr FLANNERY said it was an ansurdity to expect that the workmen would be able to conduct negotiations with clever business men. He moved that the Ceuncil should endeavour to have the original resolution again propoeed by Councillor Evans,
. . Mr BUCKLEY seconded. Mr GREALEY moved that no further action be taken for the time being, _
The SECRETaRY- seconded.

In supporting tbeattendMent, Mr PLINSTON Said he thought the reward that would be obtained would not to sufficient to justity them in forcing upon Councillor Evans the necessity of moving the resolution. tie was sorry to say that he did not think that for a long titne to come they would do any good at the municipal elections, or alter the condition of the Conned.. The thing was so far distant that he did cot thank the forc- ing of the resolution would be worth the bother. He maintained that the resolution already pissed was an advantage gained, and credit was due to toe Trades Council for having Rained so much. Mr FLANNERY said the resolution rni,h-. be all r;iztat for some societies but he contended Wit the lsbouring men ought to have their own oflicials to conduct negotia- tions for them. - . .

Mr PODMORE thought the Council should accept the undoubted advantage already gained and wait for a further opportunity to advance. The whole affair arose from statements that men had been victimised for tak- ing an active part in promoting their own welfare. He had always looked upon these cases as being authentic. With regard to the interpretation of the resolution, he asked how long the friendly, personal intercourse was going to last. To what extent would a committee take it ?

div.head: -.0.---. VOLUNTEER PARADE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: -.0.---. VOLUNTEER PARADE AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday morning in answer to an invitation from the Rev Alfred Wells:superintendent minister, the Run- corn Volunteer detachment attended divine &Irvine at St Paul's Church, Runcorn, under the command of Captain Asbton• The detachment was supported by the Runcorn Fire Brigade, under Superintendent Wright, and by the Camden boys brigade. The Rev Alfred Wells officiated at the service. The rev gentleman based his discourse on the 27ch versa Ist chapter of Philippians, " Let your donversation be such as beCometh the gospel of Christ." He said that no more appropriate counsel could be given to the homogenous gathering before him which repre- sent?d the national, political, social,businesa and religi- ous life of Runcorn. It was in Runcorn those present had to play their part as citizens. He, therefore,wished to show what their duty was and also the spirit in which that duty should be performed. lit toy persons thought they were increasing their piety by ref using to take any public office. Many even refused to give a vote at any election on the same grounds. Such, however, was not Paul's ides of piety. Paul never forgot that if he had the privileges he had also the responsibilities of a Re- manpitizen. No man could justly claim the rights of citizenship yet ignore its duties. It was not right to expect the guardianship of the police yet hold it wrong to enter the force, to sit on the Magisterial bench, Or act on the Watch Committee. Or to expect from the com- munity a supply of pure water as a right, yet wrong to give one's presmce in the management of the water works. Or that it was right for a Christian to expect protection from a standing army and navy, yet wrong for a Christian to become a soldier or a marine. It was the duty of every Christian man, whether soldier, marine, magistrate, councillor, guardian, mem- ber of the school hoard, or of the fire brigade to carry into his life and work the spirit of Christ. The Chris- tian was truest to the Christian ideal when he took his full share of the duties which made for the common good and it was his duty in his private as well as his public capacity to be always " clam handed." They should act on the tocsin of the old puritans, " For God and our country." The gospel was not simply to be believed in and obeyed, but was to be a rule of conduct. It would then he found that it gripped close and went deep down. The gospel was not only inclusive, but was exclusive also. Public men were often perplexed as to the way they ought to go for the public good. Worldly interest and:popular opi don ruled one way, but the law of Goa might rule in the opposite direction, and it was the duty of the Christian man to be loyal to God at all hazards. Mon should work for the public good without party spirit.—The rev, gentleman concluded a powerful sermon by paying a high tribute to the volunteers. During the service the National Anthem was played by the 'Volunteer Bind and joined in by the congregation. Special anthems were also rendered by the choir:

div.head: ' ACCIDENT TO A BOY.
div.p: ' ACCIDENT TO A BOY.

On Tuesday a lad named Dearden, 14 years of age, employed at the Sankey Sugar Works, slipped down some steps and in falling broke his arm and wrist and dislocated the elbow. The injured limb was attended to by Dr Gange and the lad is pro- gressing as well as can be expected. A RUNAWAY HORSE AT EARLESTOWN.

On Wednesday a horse and cart belonging to M Marsh,of Newton,were taking a load of boards from the yard of Mr <I Finning, Wargrave-road, when from some cause or other the horse became restive, and dashed off at a good speed down Wargrave- road. The driver in endeavouring to stop was knocked down, and badly shaken, but fortunately kept:clear of the wheels, and after being attended to by Dr Patterson, was able to proceed home. The beards fell from the cart and the noise caused by them falling on the ground further startled the horse which proceeded at a mad pace for some distance before it was stopped. . GOOD TEMPLAR). The Hope of Earlestown Lodge held its weekly meeting at Wargrave Hall on Monday night, when they were favoured with a visit by Bro B J George. A good number of members and friends were pro- sent, the meeting being a public one. A splendid address was given by Bro George on "Temperance and Temperance work." Songs were rendered by Mr Grissold, Miss Harrison, Sister E Woods; recita- tion by Bro J Warburton. Bro Roberts also gave a short address. Pianist, Miss Williamson.

div.head: ... DAMAGE TO CLOVER CROPS.
div.p: ... DAMAGE TO CLOVER CROPS.

Six boys named Harry Dale, Herbert Martin, Henry Martin, George Lomas, Harold Case, and George Tew,were brought before the Newton bench on Thursday on a charge of doing wilful damage to clover crops in a field belonging to Richer 1 Alder- son, of Crow-lane, Earlestown, on the 21st of June, to the extent of £l.—Mr H J Longton prosecuted, and submitted that trespassers were repeatedly do- ing damage to crops in the district. He asked for police protection for Mr Alderson.—The boys were ordered to pay the damage.

div.head: • AN- tARLESTOWN ASSAULT CASE.
div.p: • AN- tARLESTOWN ASSAULT CASE.

At Newton Petty sessions, on Thursday, morn- ing before Messrs Tid Gillespie (chairman), Colonel Wood, and J Unsworth, to young men named Richard Jones, and Ralph Vizard, were charged with assaulting John Henry hitlow. Complain- ant said that on the 3rd inst. the defendants at- tacked him in Market-street, Earlestown, knocked him down, and Jones kicked him several times.— The bench fined Jones 58 and costs, and dismissed the case against Vizard on payment of costs.

div.head: NEWTON HOMEOWNER HEAVILY FINED.
div.p: NEWTON HOMEOWNER HEAVILY FINED.

Wilfred Prescott appeared before the Newton magistrates on Thursday on a charge of cruelty to a horse. Constable Wooff said that on the 27th ult. he met the defendant with an old brown mare in Warrington Toad, Winwick. It was lame in the off hind leg from old spavin —lnspector Print said that when he examined the horse it was suffering from contracted tendons and spavin.—Questioned by the chairman (Mr Gillespie) as to what he had done with the horse, defendant said he had sold it, but didn't know how much for.—The Chairman: As you ha ye sold this poor brute we will fine you 20s and Costs. If you had destroyed it, we would have let you off a grent deal more easily.

THE CHILD MESSENGER ACT IT EARLESTOWN. mThe first case under the new Child Messenger Act was heard at Newton Petty Sessions on Thurs- day, when Mary Peppard was summoned before Messrs T J Gillespie (in the chair) and Colonel Wood for sending her son aged twelve, to a public- house for liquor. Constable Clarke said that at 8 15 on Wednesday night, the 11th June, he saw defendant's eon, aged twelve, going to the Swan Inn, Earlestown, with a pint bottle. He followed. and the lad said his mother had sent him for a pint of stour.—Defendant pleaded gaily, and said she ' was sorry she had made the mistake.—The Bench dismissed the case,ss it was the first brought under their notice, on payment of costs.

• THE HOSPITAL BAZAAR. It will be seen from an advertisement in another column that the open air bazaar in aid of funds for the provision of a Cottage Hospital will be held on the ground of the Earlestown Football club on Thursday, Friday and Saturday next week. The preparations are well advanced and by Wednesday evening it is expected that the various marquees and tents will be erected. To provide against possible damp from the ground, all the places will be boarded and made as comfortable as possible. Amusements of various kinds will be provided, and an excellent marionette show will afford entertain- ment for young and old. There will be suitable side shows, and the stalls will be laden with articles of a useful and fancy character. All that is needed for success is fine weather, and plenty of patronage.

GRANT TO AN EARLESTOWN MAN. On Saturday evening at the Hand and Banner Inn, Newton-le-Willows, an interesting gathering took place in connection with the National Equa- lized Order of Druids It will be remembered that some time back a man named Jackson met with a serious accident on Messrs Richard Evans and Co's line, Newton, the result being that both his leg were taken off He recovered from his injuries and the National Equalized Order of Druids to assist him decided to make him a grant from the compensation fund promoted by them. The sur- geon of the Lodge (Dr. Walter Latham) in the pre- sence of a large number of members, including a number of officers from Leeds,handed to Mr Jackson the sum of £6O. He said he regretted it WAS necessary to make such a grant, but he was thank- ful they were able to componsate to a slight degree Mr Jackson's suffering and loss. The reoipieat's brother acknowledged the generosity of the order. Speeches interspersed with songs were given during the evening. Sr. JOHN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, EARLESTOWN.

The annual treat to the scholars attending the above school, took place on Saturday afternoon in brilliant weather. The scholars, together with the Men's and Women's Bible Classes, assembled at the Church, where a short service was conducted by the Rev T R Matthews. Afterwards a precession was formed, and accompanied by the Viaduct Brass Band, paraded the principal streets of the town. The number in the procession was upwards of 1.800, distributed as follows :—Sunday Schuol, 1,600; Women's Bible Class, 100; Men's Bible Class, 125. The juvenile portion of the scholars were conveyed in vans. kindly lent by the L. and N.-W. Railway Company. The Irprocession finished up at the Common, where the grand stand was placed at the disposal of the school, and therein an enjoyable and substantial tea was provided. Toe teachers and members of the Mother's Meeting attended to the wants of toe children. The evening was after- wards spent in racing and games of various kinds, whilst the elder portion of the gathering indulged in dancing. The expenses of the treat were pro- vided out of the proceeds of the Christmas Tree held last December, when a sum cf £.50 was raised.

No BFTTER THAN THE BEST, but Better than the Rest. are ALF TAYLOR'S WONDBRFUL BOOTS. 45, Hors- market-street, Warrington.—Advo. A Warrington Boy Dies from Sunstroke. In the course of his sermon, on Sunday evening, the Rev W Bracecamp, vicar of St Paul's, alluded to the death of William Henry Hackett, 13 years of age, of Padgate-lane, who was formerly a member of the Sunday school. He stated that a short time ago the child went to Wales with his parents for a short holiday. He was in the garden one day for some hours. and when he returned to the house he complained that he felt unwell. He became worse and was brought to Warrington, wbere be was attended by Dr Joseph. He died in a few days,and the medical certificate recorded the fact that the death was due to sunstroke. The rev gentleman in his sermon alluded in kindly terms to the deceased, and said he had no :doubt lthe parents, who were then present, would have the sympathy of the can gregation in their sad bereavement.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST MAJOR
div.p: THE CHARGE AGAINST MAJOR
LEWIS.
Defendant Committed for Trial.

Major Richard Lewis, a justice of the peace. ex-town councillor, and one of the best known men in Widnes, made his third appearance before the Widnes magis- trates on Wednesday to answer grave accusations of falsification of accounts. The major,whose arrest caused little short of consternation in the town in which he has been for so many years prominently connected, sur- rendered shortly before half-past ten, and, as he sat in a chair alongside the legal gentlemen in the case, he appeared very dejected. The charge against him was that while he was in the employment of the Hutchinson Trustees as bookkeeper be falsified the accounts and ob- tained large sums of money. The prosecution was at the instance of Mr H T Clancey, receiver and manager of the Hutchinson estate,and his case was laid before the court by Mr Paxton, solicitor, Liverpool. The interests of the defendant were watched by Mr H L Riley. CASE FOR THE PROoECUTION. The case for the prosecution was that the defendant. had deliberately made false entries in the books in his charge with intent to defraud. Lewis was cashier and boos-keeper in the employment of the receiver and manager of the Hutchinson Estate. He had held the post for many yealcand when Captain Clancey was ap- pointed receiver and manager he was kept on. The , alleged defalcations all appeared in one account. On the 13th April a cheque was received by the defendant from the Sheffield and Midland Railway for £332 'Zs 91,usade I payable to the rec.iver and manager of the estate. The defendant had no authority to endorse the cheque, but he only entered in the cash book a sum of £2lO , 178 51, in the ledger, however, the cheque was entered as £3lO 7s sd. It was this ais- crepancy that caused investigations to be made and the fraud to be discovered. The cheque in question was actually paid into the bank, and the defendant did not embezzle any part of it, but it was alleged that this false entry was undoubtedly in- tended to conceal the fact that there was a large amount short in the cash, and that the defendant had appro- priated money to his own use. The falsification of the account was undoubtedly for a fraudulent purpose. It was successful. The fictitious entries had spread over a number of years. and had deceived the receiver and auditor for a long time. It was only in September last that the auditor called the attention of the defendant to the discrepancies,and then the defendant made a volun- tary confession to the effect that he had appropriated , something like £3,670.

" LOYAL AND SATISFACTORY. Captain Clanoey, the receiver and manager of the estate, in reply to Mr Riley, stated that the annual turnover of the estate passing through the defendant's hands was b3tween £lB,OOO and £20,000. Apart from the defalcations alleged the defendant was receiving a salary of £3OO a year, and was a perfectly loyal and satisfactory servant, always desirous, apparently, to do whatever be could.

div.head: EVIDENCE.
div.p: THE EVIDENCE.

Among a great deal of detailed evidence offered was the testimony of Mr E D White, chartered accountant, Liverpool, whose audit of the books led to the die- ' covery of the discrepancies. When witness spoke about them the defendant said the cash-book entries must be rignt but the ledger postings must be wrong. However, wuen be was asked to produce his roueh cash-book be locked it up in the safe. Later in the day the defendant offered a thither explanation, and inti- mated that he would like to speak to witness privately. The desired interview almost immediately took place, and the defendant said " I regret to tell you that neither the entries in the cash book nor the ledger are correct. The irregularities have existed in my accounts for some years ; Marmot say how many," Witness told him that tke matter would have to be vported to the receiver, and on the following day,when Captain Clancey arrived, the defendant produced a written statement. Witness had prepared a statement of the cash deficiency due to the estate from 1891 to Sep- tenther,l9oo, and showed that the amount was £3,776 Ifis 7d. Defendant had submitted to him this statement after adding to it a memorandum, which he signed. Questioned by Mr Riley, Mr White stated that in addition to accepting the summarised statement of the deficiency as substantially correct, the defendant rendered every possible assistance in tracing the various items. Lewis also indicated in what accounts to look brittle irregularities intended Ea conceal the deficiencies. , _ .

Evidence of arrest was given by Inspector Strickland. From September last up to the present time the defend- ant had resided at Litton Lodge, and had made no attempt to evade any charges that might be preferred against him...

-Jobn Valentine (agent at Widnes for Messrs Greenall, Whitley, and Co.) said his firm owned premises for which ground rent is paid to the Hutchinson estate, and pay rent in respect of same hall-yearly. In 1898 a coal- yard was rented in Peel-street, Widnes. Witness paid prisoner in March, 1898, a sum of money amounting to £5O 3s 41. A receipt (produced) was given marked "B. T. 'J. A."

div.head: DEFENDANT'S STATEMENT.
div.p: DEFENDANT'S STATEMENT.

This was all the evidence to support the charge of falsification of accounts, and before committal to the assizes the prisoner banded in a statement to be inc,,r- porated in the depositions. In it he stated that he must bow to the inevitable in the way of submitting himself for trial and, if need be. punishment. He first became connected with the Hutchinson family in 1864, and was raised from an ordinary clerk to the combined post of cashier and book- keeper. For several years the management of the estate was practically in his hands, but from 1880 to 1901 his salary of £3OO was not advanced. although without means, he rashly became the purchaser of pro- perty in Widnes for £lO,OOO, but he found the invest- ment was not as good as he expected, mainly owing to the Widnes chemical industry going down. By this speculation he had spent £2,500 more than his income. He had profited nothing by his misappropriation, and he thought with careful treatment his property could be sold advantageously. He bad a wife and five children, all in good positions, and on their behalf he pleaded for mercy. He ban resigned his connection with the local Volunteer force, which he did much to raise, and also with the Town Council. His Justice of the Peaceship must naturally be forfeited.
Upon the cliarge of falsification,and also on the charge of embr zzlement, prisoner was committed to the Liver- pool assizes, bsil being allowed in one sum of £2OO, and two SLIM Of £lOO each.

div.head: RgTURNED SOLDIERS. Runcorn's Appreciation.
div.p: THE RgTURNED SOLDIERS. Runcorn's Appreciation.
Letter from the Chairman of the Council.
The folio wing is a copy of the letter addressed Co local regulars, reservists, volunteers, Ste, by the Chairman of the Runcorn Urban Council, and the reply of Corporal Davrin.

" Dear Sir,—Tne great war io South Africa has been the means of drawing out some of the best qualities inherent in the manhood of this country. Patriotism and devotion to one's native land are characteristics which have always been highly esteemed. At the call to arms of our !ate Queen,Victeria the Good,you readily responded Co the call of duty,and have faced the dangers of wounds, disease, and death in the great Boer war, and the country is justly proud of the brave and humane manner in which its soldiers have conducted the cam- paigns. It has been universally felt that it was only fitting that the celebration of the Coronation of Ws Majesty King Edward the Seventh should be taken advantage of to Express the high appreciation which is felt by the townspeople of Runcorn for the valuable services you have rendered to your country, and I bee., on behalf of this town to ask you to accept our grateful acknowledgment and to express the hope that as honourable peace has now been made with your brave and able foes you may long be spared to witness a happy and contented South Africa as the result of your self denying Mows and of those of your brave comrades.—l have the honour to be yours faithfully. . SAMUEL TAYLOR. Chairman of the Urban District Council of Runcorn, and of the Coronation Celebration Committee. 24, Halton-road, Runcorn, July 7th, 1902. Dear Sir,—l have al kb great satisfaction received the address and cheques forwarded by you, in the name of the Urbau District Council of Runcorn, and I now take !the opportunity of tendering my heartfelt thanks for the 1 same. I (with ali my loyal comrades in arms) was I indeed grieved that the serieue illness of our King I necessitated the postponement of the festivities for which preparations were made, but we are now indeed pleased I to read that His Gracious Majesty is making such rapid strides towaeds comelete recovery. Again thanking you and the people of R acorn for giviag this honour to the soldiers of His Majesty, who have served him and his illustrious mother as well as lay in their power during the war in South Africa, now happily over,—l bave the honour to be sir, yours grate- fully,
Dd. DAVRIN, (Late Corporal R.F.A.)
